description:
The City of Milton Planning Department is authorized for two full-time code enforcement positions. Following a recent vacancy, staff evaluated the City’s current enforcement needs and determined that the community would benefit from a more visible, field-based code enforcement presence, particularly within the City’s Community Redevelopment Areas and public parks.
The City has experienced an increase in concerns involving litter, improper use of public facilities, individuals sleeping in parks and pavilions, parking violations, property maintenance, and other activities affecting the safety, appearance, and public enjoyment of these areas. Although the Milton Police Department responds when law enforcement intervention is necessary, its officers must prioritize calls for service and cannot provide a continuous presence in the City’s parks and CRA districts.
To address this need, the vacant code enforcement position was restructured as a City Ranger. The City Ranger is a civilian code enforcement employee and is not a sworn law enforcement officer. The position is intended to provide a recognizable, approachable presence in the community while supporting the Planning, Police, Public Works, and Parks and Recreation departments.
title: Funding Participation for City Ranger Position

description:
On behalf of Leadership Santa Rosa Class 39, we respectfully request the City of Milton’s support to continue feasibility planning for a solar-powered, off-grid public charging station in Milton. The project is designed as a public safety and community resilience resource, giving residents and visitors a free place to charge phones and small devices during storms, power outages, and everyday park use.
Milton has been identified as a preferred location because of the central location, the City’s importance to Santa Rosa County, and the opportunity to create a practical model that could later be expanded to other parks. At this stage, we are not asking the City to fund the project. Our class is working to secure grants, sponsorships, donations, and in-kind support for the equipment and installation.
What we are requesting now is Council’s general support and direction for City staff to help evaluate feasible siting options. Our preferred option is a standard solar charging station placed on or near a concrete pad close to a bench or high-use pedestrian area. If additional funding is raised, we would also like to evaluate a larger picnic-table-style model, which would require a larger footprint and a location that works with the city planning.
Because the estimated delivery timeline is approximately 10 weeks once ordered, we would like to begin site planning now if the project is feasible. Early coordination will help confirm the best location, installation approach, anchoring needs, ADA access, hurricane or wind-rating expectations, maintenance considerations, and any permitting or code requirements.
We view this as a modest, donor-supported infrastructure improvement with practical public benefit. It strengthens emergency preparedness, expands access to communication during outages, and enhances the daily usability of a public park. We welcome Council’s feedback and respectfully request permission to coordinate with City staff on next steps.
Requested Staff Coordination
• Identify one or more feasible locations for a standard charging station as well as for a larger picnic-table model (model will depend on funds raised).
• Confirm installation requirements, including pad placement, anchoring, ADA access, storm-resilience considerations, maintenance expectations, and permitting needs.
• Determine whether the project can align with your current planning timeline or whether an alternate City-approved location is preferred.
• Allow Leadership Santa Rosa Class 39 to continue fundraising and vendor coordination based on the City’s preferred site and model
title: Leadership Santa Rosa Class 39 Project - Solar Station (action item)

description:
The City of Milton 25-Year Vision & Master Plan began as a much more focused planning effort. Staff initially envisioned the document as an update to the City's Riverfront Redevelopment Plan, with the intent of pursuing a Community Planning Technical Assistance (CPTA) Grant to develop a new planning framework centered on downtown Milton, the Qualified Opportunity Zone, redevelopment opportunities, and future investment.
As the planning process progressed, however, it became clear that Milton's needs and opportunities extended well beyond the downtown and riverfront. Major projects were already advancing throughout the City, while additional infrastructure, housing, workforce, public safety, transportation, and community needs were emerging. Staff recognized an opportunity to take a broader view and ask a more important question: What will Milton need to successfully grow over the next 25 years?
From that question, the project evolved from a grant-focused downtown redevelopment plan into the City of Milton 25-Year Vision & Master Plan: A Strategic Framework for Growth, Investment, and Community Transformation.
The Plan builds upon projects and priorities already underway while identifying the infrastructure and investments necessary to support Milton's future. It brings together wastewater capacity, utility modernization, stormwater and resilience, housing, childcare, public safety, transportation, recreation, downtown redevelopment, tourism, economic development, and private investment within one coordinated framework.
The Plan also incorporates the City's CRA districts, Brownfield Redevelopment Area, Low-to-Moderate Income areas, and pursuit of the Qualified Opportunity Zone 2.0 designation as tools to help direct investment and leverage outside funding. Within downtown, the addition of the Mill District builds upon the Riverfront Redevelopment Plan and establishes a long-term vision for historic infill, placemaking, small-business development, and a potential transition toward Form-Based development standards inspired by Milton's early-1900s mill-town character.
Importantly, this is intended to be a living vision rather than a fixed construction schedule. Some projects are active today, some are in design or funding development, and others remain long-term concepts. As opportunities, partnerships, funding sources, and community needs change, individual projects may evolve while remaining connected to the larger vision.
Ultimately, the Plan is intended to provide continuity beyond individual projects, budget years, staff members, or elected terms. It gives future City Councils and staff a strategic framework to evaluate opportunities, pursue funding, guide development, and make investments that keep Milton moving forward in a way that remains true to the City's identity while creating new opportunities for those who call Milton home.
title: Milton 25 - 25 Year Vision & Masterplan DRAFT (action item)

description:
“Crush” was placed at Magnolia Hall on February 10, 2026, on a trial basis to encourage aluminum can recycling and promote environmental awareness. During its first five months at the site, the sculpture collected approximately 760 pounds of aluminum cans, demonstrating strong community participation and the effectiveness of the initiative.
Based on the success of the trial period, the Ocean Hour of Pensacola Board approved allowing Crush to remain on permanent loan to the Milton Garden Club for as long as the organization continues collecting cans. The Garden Club has agreed to pay all expenses associated with the permanent installation. No CRA funding is being requested.
The sculpture supports the Garden Club’s mission of environmental awareness, community education, beautification, and civic improvement. The request before the CRA is solely to authorize Crush to remain and be permanently installed as a fixture at Magnolia Hall in Downtown Milton.

description:
The Milton Mill District concept was developed as a downtown placemaking initiative intended to celebrate Milton's historic identity while creating new opportunities for community gathering, small business activity, and private investment. The concept builds upon the vision established through the 2015 Riverfront Redevelopment Plan, particularly the area identified as “The Mews,” which envisioned pedestrian-oriented spaces, smaller retail kiosks, cafés, seating areas, and mixed-use activity within the downtown core.
Following initial discussion by the Milton Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), the Mill District concept was referred to the Community Improvement Board (CIB) for additional review and consideration. The CIB reviewed the proposed design and determined that the concept was consistent with the City's previous riverfront redevelopment planning efforts and the vision established for the Mews corridor. The CIB supported moving the concept forward and recommended that it return to the CRA for further consideration.
As part of its recommendation, the CIB identified several important considerations that should guide future planning and implementation.
First, improvements should be designed to predominantly remain outside of property and right-of-way anticipated to be needed for the future FDOT U.S. Highway 90 widening project. While the timing of the widening remains outside of the City's control, the City should avoid making significant investments in permanent structures that would later need to be removed as part of the highway project.
Second, the City should continue evaluating opportunities to acquire strategically located property that could support the long-term Mill District vision. Property acquisition would provide greater flexibility to expand public spaces and, if appropriate, eventually develop the proposed Kiosk Village.
Third, the CIB recommended a phased approach, beginning with improvements to the City-owned Turtle Parking Lot. This first phase would focus on the proposed Mill Plaza, including an open-air pavilion, mill wheel fountain, landscaping, public seating, and infrastructure that could enhance activities already occurring downtown. Rather than attempting to create a new market from the ground up, the concept would build upon existing activities such as the Milton Farmers Market by providing permanent amenities that make those events more attractive, functional, and sustainable.
If the Mill Plaza proves successful and generates increased activity, the City and CRA could then evaluate advancing the Kiosk Village as a subsequent phase. This would require property acquisition, site planning, design, engineering, and construction, as well as consideration of setbacks, landscape buffers, utilities, stormwater, accessibility, and long-term operations.
The CIB also expressed support for establishing a consistent Mill District architectural theme that draws upon Milton's history as a mill town. Timber construction, brick walkways, historic-style lighting, water-wheel elements, landscaping, signage, and other design features could create a recognizable identity that is carried throughout future downtown improvements.
title: Mill District — Conceptual Design Update

description:
Proposed Unified Development Code Change presented as work in progress - UNDER REVIEW BY MILTON PLANNING BOARD - The City of Milton's Planning and Development Department is working to update the City's parking requirements. Currently, the City requires applicants to create a minimum amount of parking per a "flow chart" based on the use type, Gross Floor Area of the building, the number of expected full-time workers, and other various requirements which alter the required minimum. These varied required minimums have caused a number of issues for applicants who are trying to redevelop or infill the City's limited commercial space, especially downtown and in the surrounding area where it is largely already developed.
Currently, the proposed changes would eliminate parking minimums, allowing developers to better utilize the existing space, create more pathways for creative parking design, and lower regulatory permitting hurdles in the City's critical commercially and downtown zoned areas. This has been implemented successfully in many other municipalities, is supported by the American Planning Association, reduces urban sprawl, creates a more aesthetically pleasing, less cost intensive, more stormwater and flood friendly environment, all while understanding that the commercial developer has a more thorough and experiential level of knowledge as to what minimum parking they may require.
This language does not look to release the developers of parking reviews, parking maximums, nor environmental stewardship. To further the City and developer relationships while also creating a more walkable downtown, the City is looking to potentially create an avenue in which entities in the D-CM and R-C1 Zoning Districts would be allowed parking flexibility, to include variability in code minimums, given certain "Net Benefits" are provided to the City as part of increased parking or decreased requirements. This would be in the form of implementing privately-owned public parking spaces within lots that would also be accompanied by publicly beneficial infrastructure such as bio swales, increased green space, wider sidewalks, shade structures, benches, and other assorted "net-benefits" to offset any potential "negative" impacts such flexibility in regulations may produce. The addition of privately-owned public parking spaces would help further increase the publicly available parking stock while enhancing the aesthetic beauty and walkability of the downtown corridor.

Milton has been identified as a preferred location because of the central location, the City’s importance to Santa Rosa County, and the opportunity to create a practical model that could later be expanded to other parks. At this stage, we are not asking the City to fund the project. Our class is working to secure grants, sponsorships, donations, and in-kind support for the equipment and installation.
What we are requesting now is Council’s general support and direction for City staff to help evaluate feasible siting options. Our preferred option is a standard solar charging station placed on or near a concrete pad close to a bench or high-use pedestrian area. If additional funding is raised, we would also like to evaluate a larger picnic-table-style model, which would require a larger footprint and a location that works with the city planning.
Because the estimated delivery timeline is approximately 10 weeks once ordered, we would like to begin site planning now if the project is feasible. Early coordination will help confirm the best location, installation approach, anchoring needs, ADA access, hurricane or wind-rating expectations, maintenance considerations, and any permitting or code requirements.
We view this as a modest, donor-supported infrastructure improvement with practical public benefit. It strengthens emergency preparedness, expands access to communication during outages, and enhances the daily usability of a public park. We welcome Council’s feedback and respectfully request permission to coordinate with City staff on next steps.
Requested Staff Coordination
• Identify one or more feasible locations for a standard charging station as well as for a larger picnic-table model (model will depend on funds raised).
• Confirm installation requirements, including pad placement, anchoring, ADA access, storm-resilience considerations, maintenance expectations, and permitting needs.
• Determine whether the project can align with your current planning timeline or whether an alternate City-approved location is preferred.
• Allow Leadership Santa Rosa Class 39 to continue fundraising and vendor coordination based on the City’s preferred site and model

description:
Over the past several years, the City of Milton has made significant investments in downtown revitalization, including enhancements to public spaces, infrastructure improvements, and expanded programming such as community events along the riverfront. These efforts are designed to stimulate private investment, increase foot traffic, and position Milton as a desirable destination for residents, businesses, and visitors.
Despite this progress, many vacant and deteriorating structures remain, creating barriers to continued growth. These properties often:
Remain unmaintained for extended periods
Become targets for vandalism or unauthorized entry
Create safety hazards for adjacent properties and the public
Suppress nearby property values and redevelopment potential
Require disproportionate City resources for monitoring and enforcement
Currently, the City lacks a formal tracking and accountability system specifically for vacant and abandoned properties. Code Enforcement operates actively, addressing complaints as well as proactively managing problem properties, but no formal system is in place to assist them with property information.
This ordinance introduces a structured, enforceable program that:
Identifies and tracks vacant properties through mandatory registration
Requires minimum maintenance and security standards
Assigns clear responsibility to property owners and lenders
Implements a fee structure that incentivizes timely action
Provides Code Enforcement with stronger compliance tools under Chapter 162, Florida Statutes
Additionally, the ordinance aligns with Florida Statute 705.1015, reinforcing local authority to manage abandoned property conditions impacting public welfare.
KEY COMPONENTS OF THE ORDINANCEMandatory Registration:Required for properties vacant for more than 90 days, abandoned properties, and those in foreclosure.
Escalating Fee Structure:Annual fees increase the longer a property remains vacant, incentivizing redevelopment or sale.
Maintenance Requirements:Property owners must secure, maintain, and properly manage properties in compliance with City Code.
Local Contact Requirement:Ensures a responsible party is available for immediate response.
Code Enforcement Administration:Program oversight, inspections, and enforcement are handled by City staff.
STRATEGIC IMPACTThis ordinance supports:
Downtown revitalization and CRA objectives
Economic development and private investment attraction
Public safety and neighborhood stabilization
Efficient use of City resources
It supports Milton to move from reactive enforcement to a proactive redevelopment strategy.

description:
The City of Milton 25-Year Vision & Master Plan began as a much more focused planning effort. Staff initially envisioned the document as an update to the City's Riverfront Redevelopment Plan, with the intent of pursuing a Community Planning Technical Assistance (CPTA) Grant to develop a new planning framework centered on downtown Milton, the Qualified Opportunity Zone, redevelopment opportunities, and future investment.
As the planning process progressed, however, it became clear that Milton's needs and opportunities extended well beyond the downtown and riverfront. Major projects were already advancing throughout the City, while additional infrastructure, housing, workforce, public safety, transportation, and community needs were emerging. Staff recognized an opportunity to take a broader view and ask a more important question: What will Milton need to successfully grow over the next 25 years?
From that question, the project evolved from a grant-focused downtown redevelopment plan into the City of Milton 25-Year Vision & Master Plan: A Strategic Framework for Growth, Investment, and Community Transformation.
The Plan builds upon projects and priorities already underway while identifying the infrastructure and investments necessary to support Milton's future. It brings together wastewater capacity, utility modernization, stormwater and resilience, housing, childcare, public safety, transportation, recreation, downtown redevelopment, tourism, economic development, and private investment within one coordinated framework.
The Plan also incorporates the City's CRA districts, Brownfield Redevelopment Area, Low-to-Moderate Income areas, and pursuit of the Qualified Opportunity Zone 2.0 designation as tools to help direct investment and leverage outside funding. Within downtown, the addition of the Mill District builds upon the Riverfront Redevelopment Plan and establishes a long-term vision for historic infill, placemaking, small-business development, and a potential transition toward Form-Based development standards inspired by Milton's early-1900s mill-town character.
Importantly, this is intended to be a living vision rather than a fixed construction schedule. Some projects are active today, some are in design or funding development, and others remain long-term concepts. As opportunities, partnerships, funding sources, and community needs change, individual projects may evolve while remaining connected to the larger vision.
Ultimately, the Plan is intended to provide continuity beyond individual projects, budget years, staff members, or elected terms. It gives future City Councils and staff a strategic framework to evaluate opportunities, pursue funding, guide development, and make investments that keep Milton moving forward in a way that remains true to the City's identity while creating new opportunities for those who call Milton home.

description:
The City of Milton is the co-owner with Santa Rosa County of two parcels along U.S. Highway 90 (Caroline Street). The two parcels are currently used for public parking. Known as the "Turtle" Parking Lot, parcels are approximately 0.594 acres. The two parcels are separated by a Right-Of-Way of approximately 1.9 acres. Including the ROW, the total land area is 0.784 acres. The combined value of the two parcels, according to the County Property Appraiser, is $135,450. The ROW is not valued by the Property Appraiser. However, a vacant, privately owned parcel, directly across Elmira Street from the "Turtle Lot" is currently for sale at a price of $110,000 for 0.14 acres. If valued at the same price per acre, the "Turtle Lot" would be valued at $466,714. If the ROW is included, the value rises to an estimated $616,000 for the 0.784 acres.
On May 9, 2024, the Board of County Commission approved a use agreement with the City for the former Whittle Property (attached). The City paid for the improvements and ongoing upkeep of the space that is used as a passive park. The City has no ownership or lease rights to the Whittle Property and will be able to remove the picnic tables and vegetation, which can be used at other City facilities.
The County is requesting the City join with them in donating the "Turtle Lot" parcels to the State of Florida to be used in the proposed widening of Highway 90. If approved, the City could also abandon the Right-Of-Way. If abandoned, the property would be added to the adjacent parcels, both owned by the City and County, thus allowing the donation of the entire 0.784 acres.
This requested action is consistent with City Policy for the Disposition of Surplus Property, specifically Page 6, Section C - Surplus Property Not Designated for Affordable Housing (attached).
Santa Rosa County has agreed to provide any required surveying, legal documentation and filings for the abandonment, should Council choose to go forward.
This request was discussed that the July 23, 2026 Council Workshop. The majority of Council expressed support for the donation provided the City be allowed to continue to utilize the properties until such time as the State widening project commences. The County Staff present at the meeting confirmed that the current uses would be allowed and conveyance would be done via a delayed transfer agreement which clearly sets out the timeline for the project. The transfer agreement would return to Council for final approval.
title: Santa Rosa County Request - Donation of Parcels for Highway 90 Widening Project

description:
On 5/15/2026, the City of Milton applied for the FDEM Hazard Mitigation Grant Program's "Watershed Planning Program" grant, with the goal to develop a Watershed Master Plan for the City of Milton. The grant project total is $130,641, with $97,980 (75%) covered by the Federal Share and $32,661 (25%) covered ny "in-kind" matching. The City of Milton received support from the Local Mitigation Strategy (LMS) group, worked with the University of West Florida who agreed to be partner to the implementation of the grant and provide "in-kind" services, and the City was ultimately chosen as a recipient of the grant awards.
The project will focus on evaluating and planning watershed and stormwater solutions for Milton, including CRA Districts and the Historic District, where existing stormwater infrastructure has reached capacity and flood risk is increasing due to riverine flooding, sea level rise, and anticipated redevelopment. The planning effort will include hydrologic and hydraulic analyses to assess runoff volumes, storage capacity, and water quality impacts. The proximity of the Blackwater River, an Outstanding Florida Water, to the City of Milton and Milton’s CRA, Downtown, and Historic areas creates a more urgent and impactful need for such planning. A key component of the project is the evaluation of approximately 7.5 acres of City-owned land that will become available following the decommissioning of the existing wastewater treatment facility. Restricted from development by FEMA floodplain regulations, this site presents a unique opportunity for regional stormwater storage, flood attenuation, and water quality treatment. Hydrologic and hydraulic modeling will determine feasibility, design parameters, and integration with surrounding watershed systems. The Watershed Master Plan will identify priority mitigation projects, establish phased implementation strategies, and produce grant-ready documentation to support future funding applications. Watershed planning will provide the City of Milton a community approach to making decisions that ultimately aim to reduce flooding and NFIP claims.
title: FDEM - Watershed Master Plan Grant Agreement

description:
On 5/15/2026, the City of Milton applied for the FDEM Hazard Mitigation Grant Program's "Stormwater Master Plan" grant, with the goal to develop a Stormwater Master Plan for the City of Milton. The grant project total is $165,6524, with $124,143 (75%) covered by the Federal Share and $41,381 (25%) covered ny "in-kind" matching. The City of Milton received support from the Local Mitigation Strategy (LMS) group, worked with the University of West Florida who agreed to be a partner in the implementation of the grant and provide "in-kind" services, and the City was ultimately chosen as a recipient of the grant awards.
The project will focus on evaluating and planning stormwater solutions for Milton, including CRA Districts and the Historic District, where existing stormwater infrastructure has reached capacity and flood risk is increasing due to riverine flooding, sea level rise, and anticipated redevelopment. The planning effort will include hydrologic and hydraulic analyses to assess runoff volumes, storage capacity, and water quality impacts. The proximity of the Blackwater River, an Outstanding Florida Water, to the City of Milton and Milton’s CRA, Downtown, and Historic areas creates a more urgent and impactful need for such planning. A key component of the project is the evaluation of approximately 7.5 acres of City-owned land that will become available following the decommissioning of the existing wastewater treatment facility. Restricted from development by FEMA floodplain regulations, this site presents a unique opportunity for regional stormwater storage, flood attenuation, and water quality treatment. Hydrologic and hydraulic modeling will determine feasibility, design parameters, and integration with surrounding watershed systems. The Stormwater Master Plan will identify priority mitigation projects, establish phased implementation strategies, and produce grant-ready documentation to support future funding applications. Stormwater master planning will provide the City of Milton a community approach to making decisions that ultimately aim to reduce flooding and NFIP claims.
The Stormwater Master Plan (SWMP) will have citywide applicability and will benefit the entirety of the City of Milton. At present, there are no planned or ongoing projects within the City that would impede or delay the development of the SWMP. Currently, the City of Milton and the University of West Florida (UWF) are collaborating through the Pensacola and Perdido Bay Estuary Program’s Community Grant Program on the development of the Carpenter’s Stream Remediation Plan. This effort is focused on addressing hydrologic and ecological impacts resulting from off‑site nutrient loading and development‑related inputs that have adversely affected the stream’s natural function. The Carpenter’s Stream Remediation Plan will directly support development of the WMP and SWMP, particularly within and around the Carpenter’s Park area. Data, analyses, and findings generated through the remediation planning process will be leveraged, where appropriate, to inform watershed‑wide conditions, refine assumptions, and enhance the overall technical foundation of the SWMP and WMP. This coordination will improve efficiency, reduce duplication of effort, and strengthen the scientific basis of the City’s watershed planning efforts.
title: FDEM - Stormwater Master Plan Grant

description: The United States Deputy Sheriffs' Association has awarded the Police Department a grant consisting of two vehicle spike strip sets with an estimated value of $494.00 per set, for a total grant value of $988.00. Spike strips are a critical law enforcement tool used to safely end vehicle pursuits by gradually deflating a fleeing vehicle's tires, reducing the likelihood of high-speed crashes and injuries to officers, motorists, and the public. Having reliable, modern spike strips provides officers with an effective, less-lethal option to safely bring dangerous pursuits to a conclusion while minimizing risk. The Police Department's current spike strips were purchased more than twenty years ago and are now antiquated. They are significantly beyond the manufacturer's recommended service life and warranty period and have deteriorated to the point that they are no longer considered reliable or suitable for operational use. Replacing this equipment is necessary to ensure officers have dependable pursuit intervention equipment when needed.

description:
The Milton Mill DistrictA Modern Interpretation of the 2015 Riverfront Redevelopment Vision​
The Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) has long identified placemaking, historic preservation, economic development, and downtown revitalization as guiding principles for investment within the Downtown Milton Community Redevelopment Area. As the City continues to advance transformative initiatives, including the Milton Marina Redevelopment, the Bayou District mixed-use redevelopment, and future improvements along the U.S. Highway 90 corridor, staff has begun evaluating opportunities to create vibrant public spaces that encourage investment, entrepreneurship, tourism, and year-round community activity.
The proposed Milton Mill District is not intended to replace previous planning efforts, but rather to build upon and implement recommendations that have been identified through multiple City planning initiatives over the past decade.
One of the most significant examples is the 2015 Riverfront Redevelopment Plan, which envisioned a downtown destination known as "The Mews." The plan identified the block surrounding Elmira Street, Santa Rosa Street, Willing Street, and Caroline Street as one of the City's greatest opportunities for infill redevelopment and placemaking. The vision called for the creation of an internal pedestrian-oriented district that would organize new development around attractive public gathering spaces while supporting small-scale retail, cafés, outdoor seating, vendor kiosks, and mixed-use development with residential, office, and commercial uses. Rather than focusing solely on buildings, the Riverfront Redevelopment Plan emphasized creating memorable public places where people could gather, shop, dine, and experience Downtown Milton.
More recently, the Community Improvement Board's Downtown Vision Update reaffirmed many of these same objectives by identifying opportunities to strengthen walkability, activate underutilized public spaces, enhance downtown aesthetics, encourage entrepreneurship, improve public gathering areas, and establish stronger connections between the downtown core, the Blackwater River, and future redevelopment projects.
The proposed Milton Mill District represents a modern interpretation of these long-standing community goals. Inspired by Milton's historic identity as a lumber and mill town, the concept expands upon the original vision of The Mews by creating two complementary public destinations located on opposite sides of Elmira Street. Together, these spaces would establish a walkable downtown district that celebrates Milton's history while creating new opportunities for small businesses, community events, tourism, and public investment.
The first component, the Mill Plaza, would transform the City-owned Turtle Parking Lot into a flexible civic gathering space featuring an open-air timber pavilion, a mill wheel fountain, decorative vendor tables, brick streetscapes, and landscaped public seating areas for markets, festivals, and community events.
Across Elmira Street, the second component, the Kiosk Village, would build upon the original Mews concept by creating a collection of historically inspired retail kiosks designed to provide affordable opportunities for local entrepreneurs, artisans, cafés, and specialty retailers. Together, these two projects would create a unified downtown destination while reinforcing the City's continued commitment to implementing the vision established in previous planning efforts.
By advancing the Mill District concept, the CRA has the opportunity to transition from planning to implementation—creating a signature destination that connects the historic downtown, future Bayou District redevelopment, Milton Marina, and Blackwater River into one cohesive, walkable district that reflects Milton's heritage while supporting its future growth.
​

description: The Planning and Development Department, along with Chief Reble, has spent the past several months researching, demoing, and talking with other municipalities about potential online permitting portals. MGO (My Government Online) has been chosen through this process. They currently serve Santa Rosa County, which would offer a more streamlined experience for applicants that must apply to both the City and County. MGO offers the most affordable price points, is known for having a high-quality product, and offers all the necessary services for the City of Milton's Planning and Development Department, Milton Fire Department, and Code Enforcement. City staff is looking to adopt 5 modules at "Per Month" Rates; Permits & Licensing (300/month), GIS/Addressing Integration ($230/month), Code Enforcement ($100/month), Fire Inspection ($200/month), and Planning and Zoning ($200/month). This comes out to a total monthly cost of $1,030 which is approximately $12,360/year. The only upfront cost is a 25% deposit fee before implementation. No implementation fees are included, unlike all the other portal suppliers, with the remaining 75% charged after implementation (on a per-month basis). The City of Milton, if adopted, would enter into an Interlocal Agreement with MGO as they are an official entity of the State of Louisiana, making them a revenue neutral entity. Adopting an online portal will give the citizens and applicants of the City of Milton a more clear, concise, transparent, and efficient permitting experience. Additionally, and crucially, project management for City staff will be standardized, reliance on paper will be reduced, reducing the need for ever-increasing storage, and overall modernized.
title: MGO - Planning and Development Online Permitting Portal - $12,360 (action item)

description:
On March 10, 2026, the Milton City Council approved an Initial Term Sheet with Jones South Development for the redevelopment of the Milton Marina. The agreement provided a 120-day pre-development period for Jones South Development to conduct due diligence, evaluate project feasibility, and prepare a conceptual redevelopment plan for the property. During this period, the developer completed preliminary site investigations, coordinated with City staff, and continued evaluating the financial and regulatory requirements necessary to advance the project.
As the due diligence period concluded, Jones South Development notified the City of its intent to proceed with the project. While development timelines have been impacted by increased construction costs, material pricing, financing considerations, and extended permitting review periods experienced throughout the industry, the developer has continued making progress toward a comprehensive redevelopment proposal. City staff believes the project remains consistent with the Council's vision for transforming the Milton Marina into a premier waterfront destination and recommends continuing the collaborative development process.
At the July 14, 2026, City Council Workshop, Jones South Development will present its conceptual redevelopment plan, providing Council with an overview of the project vision, progress completed during the due diligence period, and anticipated next steps. The conceptual presentation is intended to provide Council with a project update and does not constitute final development approval.
In accordance with the Initial Term Sheet, Jones South Development will also remit the first year's lease payment as evidence of its continued commitment to the project. These funds will be accepted by the City and reserved exclusively for the purposes outlined within the executed agreement.

description:
Grant #1 – Patrick Leahy Bulletproof Vest Partnership (BVP) Grant
The Patrick Leahy Bulletproof Vest Partnership (BVP) Program, established by the Bulletproof Vest Partnership Grant Act of 1998 and administered by the Bureau of Justice Assistance, reimburses up to 50 percent of the cost of qualifying ballistic vests purchased for law enforcement officers. The Milton Police Department was awarded $5,274.89 through this highly competitive program. Of the 312 law enforcement agencies in Florida, only 115 received funding during this grant cycle, and MPD is proud to be among those selected. The grant funding will be used to purchase three ballistic vests with associated inner and outer carriers. Ballistic vests have a recommended service life and five-year warranty, requiring periodic replacement to ensure officers remain protected. Several current MPD vests have reached the end of their service life and require replacement. Acceptance of this grant will allow the department to transition officers to current Level IIIA soft body armor, providing enhanced protection against common handgun threats while remaining lightweight and flexible for daily patrol operations. Because ballistic vest purchases are already included in the department's annual uniform budget, the reimbursement will return funds to the City that can be utilized to replace additional aging vests and further improve officer safety.
Grant #2 – Florida Municipal Insurance Trust (FMIT) Safety Grant
The Florida Municipal Insurance Trust (FMIT) Safety Grant Program provides a 50 percent reimbursement for safety and health-related equipment that reduces workplace risk and improves employee safety. MPD was awarded funding to reimburse 50 percent of the cost of purchasing high-visibility rain jackets for the department's 21 sworn officers. The total project cost is $2,255.00, with an anticipated reimbursement of $1,127.50. MPD officers routinely respond to traffic crashes, disabled vehicles, traffic control assignments, and emergency incidents during inclement weather and low-light conditions. These situations place officers in close proximity to moving traffic, creating a significant risk of struck-by incidents. The requested jackets meet ANSI/ISEA 107-2020 Type P, Class 3 visibility standards and are specifically designed for law enforcement use. Unlike the limited rain gear currently available, these jackets accommodate duty belts and equipment while allowing immediate access to radios, firearms, and other essential tools through specialized access openings. Most MPD officers have not been issued rain jackets, and the few currently assigned are using surplus jackets originally issued by the City's Streets Department, which do not properly fit or safely accommodate law enforcement equipment. Providing every officer with properly designed, high-visibility rain gear will improve roadside safety, reduce weather-related hazards, and ensure officers remain visible and fully operational during critical incidents.
The Milton Police Department remains committed to being responsible stewards of the public funds entrusted to us. I will continue to actively pursue federal, state, local, and private grant opportunities to reduce costs to the City while ensuring my officers are equipped with the modern equipment necessary to safely and effectively serve our community.
title: MPD - Acceptance of (2) Grant Awards - $6,402.39 (action item)

description:
The City of Milton has made significant investments in decorative street lighting throughout the Downtown Historic District as part of ongoing revitalization and placemaking initiatives within the Community Redevelopment Area. Decorative Acorn-style street lamps have become a defining visual feature of downtown Milton and contribute to the district’s historic character, pedestrian experience, and overall sense of place.
Currently, the City owns and maintains more than 200 decorative Acorn street lamps throughout downtown Milton. Historically, the City has directly purchased and maintained these fixtures, with replacement costs averaging approximately $4,000 per lamp. As the decorative lighting network continues to expand, the long-term maintenance and replacement obligations associated with City-owned infrastructure have increased substantially.
To address these growing costs while continuing to enhance downtown infrastructure, the City is transitioning toward a partnership model with Florida Power & Light for future decorative lighting installations within the CRA district. Under this approach, FPL will own, install, and maintain the lighting infrastructure while the City pays a recurring monthly service fee. This model significantly reduces the City’s long-term capital replacement obligations while ensuring professional maintenance and operational reliability.
The proposed Pine Street lighting project represents the continuation of this strategy and supports broader CRA goals related to downtown connectivity, pedestrian infrastructure, historic preservation, and economic vitality. The installation will help bridge gaps in decorative lighting coverage between established downtown corridors and adjacent areas that currently lack pedestrian-scale lighting improvements.
The contracted monthly service cost from FPL is - Additional Lighting Charges $122.60, and the 10 Granville 39 Watt 4000K Black posts and post tops at $347.50, for 10 lamps includes:
Decorative Acorn-style fixtures and poles approved by the CRA and Historic Preservation Board
Installation of all conduit and conductor infrastructure
Energy and fuel costs
Ongoing maintenance and repair responsibilities
The decorative fixtures are proposed for installation approximately every 130 feet along Pine Street from Elmira Street to Combs Street.
This Agreement shall be for a term of ten (10) years from the date of initiation of service and shall extend thereafter for further successive periods of five (5) years from the expiration. Contract ​terms are attached in the packet.
Approval of this item will authorize staff to move forward with the execution of the agreement with Florida Power & Light and begin material procurement and project scheduling.
title: Pine Street Decorative Lighting Installation - CRA Proposal

attachments.name: City of Milton's Sanitation Services Narrative

description:
The City of Milton operates a comprehensive residential sanitation program that provides twice-a-week household waste collection, yard debris collection, bulk waste services, and annual community cleanup events. These services are delivered through a City-operated sanitation division utilizing specialized collection vehicles, equipment, and personnel dedicated to maintaining reliable service for residents.
Over the past several years, sanitation rate adjustments have generally been limited to inflationary increases. While these adjustments have assisted in offsetting increases in disposal costs and routine operational expenses, they have not kept pace with the broader cost increases experienced by the City. Significant growth in employee health insurance premiums, workers’ compensation expenses, equipment maintenance costs, fuel prices, and future fleet replacement needs has placed increasing pressure on the sanitation fund.
A review of comparable service providers demonstrates that the City currently charges substantially less than private-sector competitors while providing a comparable or greater level of service. Current residential sanitation rates are approximately $23.76 per month, compared to rates exceeding $30 per month among competing providers. When evaluated on a per-collection basis, Milton continues to provide one of the lowest-cost sanitation services in the market.
To address these financial challenges while avoiding a substantial one-time increase, staff evaluated a phased implementation strategy. Under the proposed approach, residential sanitation rates would increase by 10% annually for three years, in addition to standard inflationary adjustments. This strategy allows the City to gradually improve cost recovery, strengthen the long-term sustainability of the sanitation enterprise fund, and establish funding capacity for future equipment replacement and operational needs.
Staff believes this measured and predictable approach balances fiscal responsibility with affordability while ensuring residents continue to receive high-quality sanitation services at a competitive rate.
Staff is requesting Council input and direction ​in order to ​accurately prepare the FY 2027 Sanitation ​Department Budget. If approved, the rate increase would take ​effect with the new fiscal year, October 1, 2026.
title: Sanitation Rate Adjustment Proposal (information item)

description:
The Police Department respectfully requests authorization to accept the donation and transfer of approximately $19,000 in tactical equipment from the Winter Springs Police Department. The donated equipment includes seven ballistic shields (estimated value of $1,700 per unit), one tactical blanket (estimated value of $1,000), and seven ballistic helmets (estimated value of $900 per helmet).
These items have exceeded the manufacturer’s recommended warranty or service life and are being disposed of by the originating agency. However, based on operational knowledge and assessment, the ballistic properties of the equipment remain functional and usable for law enforcement purposes. While these items may not represent ideal long-term equipment solutions, they will provide a valuable supplement to the Department’s current resources until additional funding can be secured to fully equip personnel with new equipment.
The Department recognizes that expired ballistic equipment is not a perfect solution; however, an expired ballistic shield is significantly better than having no shield available during critical incidents. This equipment will enhance officer safety and improve operational readiness when responding to active shooter incidents, barricaded subjects, high-risk building searches, and open-door house checks.
The equipment is being donated and transferred to the Department at no cost to the City or the Police Department. The only associated expense is the personal time voluntarily donated by the Chief to coordinate and retrieve the equipment and support assistance for the Winter Springs Police Department.
Acceptance of this donation will provide immediate operational and safety benefits to officers serving the community while allowing the Department additional time to pursue grant opportunities and budget funding for replacement equipment.

description:
The City of Milton has made significant investments in decorative street lighting throughout the Downtown Historic District as part of ongoing revitalization and placemaking initiatives within the Community Redevelopment Area. Decorative Acorn-style streetlamps have become a defining visual feature of downtown Milton and contribute to the district’s historic character, pedestrian experience, and overall sense of place.
Currently, the City owns and maintains more than 200 decorative Acorn street lamps throughout downtown Milton. Historically, the City has directly purchased and maintained these fixtures, with replacement costs averaging approximately $4,000 per lamp. As the decorative lighting network continues to expand, the long-term maintenance and replacement obligations associated with City-owned infrastructure have increased substantially.
To address these growing costs while continuing to enhance downtown infrastructure, the City is transitioning toward a partnership model with Florida Power & Light for future decorative lighting installations within the CRA district. Under this approach, FPL will own, install, and maintain the lighting infrastructure while the City pays a recurring monthly service fee. This model significantly reduces the City’s long-term capital replacement obligations while ensuring professional maintenance and operational reliability.
The proposed Pine Street lighting project represents the continuation of this strategy and supports broader CRA goals related to downtown connectivity, pedestrian infrastructure, historic preservation, and economic vitality. The installation will help bridge gaps in decorative lighting coverage between established downtown corridors and adjacent areas that currently lack pedestrian-scale lighting improvements.
The proposed monthly service cost from FPL is $122.60 for 10 lamps and includes:
Decorative Acorn-style fixtures and poles approved by the CRA and Historic Preservation Board
Installation of all conduit and conductor infrastructure
Energy and fuel costs
Ongoing maintenance and repair responsibilities
The decorative fixtures are proposed for installation approximately every 130 feet along Pine Street from Elmira Street to Combs Street.
Approval of this item will authorize staff to proceed with the execution of the agreement with Florida Power & Light and to begin material procurement and project scheduling.
title: Pine Street Decorative Lighting Installation (action item)

description:
Operation Safety Cone was launched in 2025 as a collaborative community policing initiative designed to strengthen relationships between the Milton Police Department and the community’s youth through positive engagement and proactive interaction. The program allows officers to distribute ice cream cone vouchers to children observed demonstrating safe habits and positive community behavior, including:
Wearing bicycle helmets
Properly using sidewalks and crosswalks
Practicing safe pedestrian habits
Picking up litter
Demonstrating respectful and responsible conduct
The program was originally developed to reinforce the principles of community-oriented policing while creating approachable and positive interactions between law enforcement officers and local families. In addition to its public safety and community engagement objectives, the initiative also supports economic activity within the Downtown Community Redevelopment Area by directing participating families to locally owned businesses.
The original 2025 CRA agenda item identified the program’s benefits as strengthening trust between law enforcement and youth, increasing community engagement, and supporting downtown businesses through voucher redemption activity.
In 2025, the CRA approved $1,000 to support the program. Supporting invoices demonstrate that the project costs exceeded the approved funding level. An invoice from the participating ice cream vendor totaled $1,000 alone for approximately 1,000 ice cream servings. Additional printing and production costs associated with promotional and redemption cards totaled more than $100. Other departments ultimately assisted in covering portions of the project expenses to ensure successful implementation.
For 2026, the Milton Police Department proposes expanding the initiative and anticipates increased participation levels throughout the community. Additionally, the City has transitioned to a new vendor partnership with Scoops Ice Cream in downtown Milton. Due to rising supply costs and vendor pricing changes, the projected cost per redemption item has increased from approximately $1 per cup during the 2025 program to approximately $3 per cone for the 2026 program.
The requested increase in CRA funding to $2,000 will help offset projected increases in:
Ice cream redemption costs
Printing and promotional materials
Administrative support expenses
Program marketing and outreach
Miscellaneous operational supplies
The Operation Safety Cone initiative directly aligns with the CRA’s goals of promoting community engagement, enhancing downtown activity, supporting local businesses, and improving the overall quality of life within the redevelopment district. The program also continues to build upon the significant public attention and positive community response generated during the inaugural 2025 initiative.
title: Operation Safety Cone - 2026 Community Policing Initiative (action item)

description:
As the City nears completion of the design, engineering and permitting process for the new wastewater treatment plant and disposal area, the project is on schedule to be bid in the summer of 2026.
As such, staff, along with Donovan-Hill Group, has developed a preliminary estimate that will be presented at the Special Called Meeting on May 28, 2026.
For years, the City has been amassing reserves for the purpose of removing the treated effluent from the Blackwater River and replacing the aging wastewater treatment plant.
As of May 12, 2026, the City has amassed the following reserves:
1. General Fund Cash Reserves $1,026,029
2. General Fund Invested Reserves $8,147,115
3. Water & Sewer Restricted Invested Reserves $3,352,292
4. Water & Sewer Fund Invested Reserves $5,074,092
5. Water & Sewer Residential Impact Fees $602,835
6. Water & Sewer Commercial Impact Fees $343,210
7. Sewer Residential Impact Fees $5,314,664
8. Sewer Commercial Impact Fees $5,390,048
TOTAL RESERVES $29,250,285
As per City Policy, the General Fund and Water & Sewer Fund must maintain 4.5 months of operating capital on hand at all times. For the General Fund that amount is $3,000,000. For the Water & Sewer Fund, the reserve is $2,200,000. Subtracting the required reserves from the amount available, the total amount of reserves available to be dedicated to the new wastewater treatment plant and disposal areas is $24,050,285. All reserve funds will continue to grow as interest is accrued until the funds are expended over the course of the project, which will span three to five years.
This agenda item is not requesting the expenditure of any funds at this time. Staff is requesting Council officially designate a minimum of $24,050,285 of City Reserve Funds for the new wastewater treatment plant and disposal areas, plus interest accrued during construction. This official designation will allow the City to demonstrate to external funding sources that the matching funds for grant applications are not only available, but dedicated to the project by official act of Council. This will also prohibit the use of these funds for other projects, unless approved by a majority vote of Council.

description:
During the due diligence and permitting process for the new wastewater treatment plant, pipeline and disposal areas, Donovan-Hill Group (formerly Baskerville Donovan) identified the burrows of a protected species, the gopher tortoise, on the City's properties. As such, the City is required to mitigate any threats to the tortoise. The standard practice for this species is to relocate the animals to an approved, long-term recipient site. A permit for this activity must be secured from the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission. This work must be conducted by a certified FWC Authorized Gopher Tortoise Agent. Six (6) potential burrows were identified on the effluent disposal site #2 and three (3) along the effluent pipeline route. The cost for permitting and capture of the tortoises is $15,180 ($10,175 for Site 2 and $5,005 for the pipeline).
In addition to the permitting and capture costs, the permit application fees and re-homing costs are as follows:
Effluent Pipeline: Permit Fee: $273
Re-Homing fee: $13,500
Disposal Site#2: Permit Fee: $683
Re-Homing Fee: $27,000
TOTAL: $41,456
The re-homing cost per tortoise is $4,500 per adult and $1,500 per juvenile. This represents the cost to re-home if each of the nine burrows is occupied by an adult tortoise. This will not be known until the permit is secured and capture initiated. The City will pay these costs directly with no mark-up from Donovan-Hill Group.
The total maximum cost for the two gopher tortoise relocation Task Orders is $56,636.

description:
New Board and Committee appointments must now meet the requirements of the ordinances as passed during the 1/13/2026 and 4/14/2026 City Council Meetings. In doing so, each board will need to be reviewed and appointed by Council. Staff has created a means to do this as a "Year One" scenario. The "Year One" scenario is as described below;
Treat the new 2026 ordinance as a "Year One" appointment ordinance which would allow each member that is eligible to continue to serve if they so choose, subject to Council reappointment.
Each board will follow the same set-up as the Milton Planning Board - Members will be appointed as voted on and agreed by the 2 Council members of each Ward, One Mayor-at-Large appointment, and Two Council-At-Large appointments for a total of 7 members serving on each board. The attached spreadsheet shows potential "appointment rotations" and appointees based on each potential member's seat. If Council so chooses, the Mayor & Council At-Large seats may be filled with current members. Appointment of members that are to fill Ward-specific seats should be rated based on favoring those who reside in that Ward, then those that live within the City of Milton, then those that reside in Santa Rosa County, and finally any other criteria supporting the potential members nomination (preference for 1. In ward, 2. In City, 3. In Santa Rosa County).
Council will need to reappoint the eligible members on a 3-year staggered basis. The new "Year One" appointments will need to be scheduled as presented below in the 2 possible scenarios or as Council sees fit. Council will need to decide which stagger scenario is preferred.
After the initial "Year One" rotation, every appointment to every board will be on a 3-year service term, which fulfills the 3-year staggered appointments. (After the first "Year One" 2-year appointments are complete, any future appointment in that seat is on a 3-year rotation)
Each board will have an "Expiration Month". This will create a more cohesive, consistent, and repeatable appointment schedule. Staff recommends: Community Improvement Board - Expiration Month is March with new terms beginning in April. Board of Adjustments - Expiration Month is May and terms beginning in June. Historic Preservation Board - Expiration Month is July with terms beginning in August. Planning Board - Expiration Month September with terms beginning in October.
New appointments after the "Year One" scenario will need to be able to achieve the "Staggered 3-year" term limit. In order to achieve this, the first round of appointments will need to have staggered years of appointments followed by any future appointments being for 3-years. City staff has developed two possible paths in order to do so.
1. 3/4 Seat Stagger - 3 appointments will fill a shortened 2-year term with the usual 3-year term after appointment, and 4 appointments will fill a full 3-year term. This will allow all future 3-year appointments to be staggered in such a manner that 2 consecutive years of appointments will occur with one year of no new appointments. The pattern would repeat; appointments in year four and five, with no new appointments in year six and so on. Again, after the first initial 3, 2-year terms, no more 2-year appointments will be necessary and every appointment from then on will be for the usual 3-years.
2. 2/2/3 Seat Stagger with appointments taking place every year.
In a 2/2/3 Seat Stagger: Group 1 would consist of Ward 1, Council At-Large 1 for one, 1-year term; Group 2 Ward 2, Council At-Large 2 for one, 2-year term; Group 3 Ward 3, Ward 4, Mayor At-Large for one, 3-year term. Each would be appointed for a three-year term thereafter, per usual.
Again, as stated in both scenarios, the non-3-year terms would only occur once, during the "Year One", in order to create the staggered effect. Every appointment after will be the normal 3-year term.
If Council desires, all current Board members can be reappointed to their respective boards under either the 3/4 or 2/2/3 rotation. Staff has developed a recommendation for each seat in each Board with the current membership. This recommendation identifies which seat the current member is filling, and the new term they will serve. If Council adopts this recommendation and the Expiration Month concept, each board will continue as currently configured with the start month for each new term adjusted. Council would not have to make any appointments for any board, other than for vacancies, for one or two years, depending on the rotation schedule selected.
title: Board Appointment Reorganization Plan (action item)

description:
Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRAs) play a critical role in addressing blight, promoting economic development, and reinvesting in targeted areas through tools such as Tax Increment Financing (TIF). Effective CRA governance requires a clear understanding of statutory requirements, financial oversight, redevelopment planning, and public accountability.
The Florida Redevelopment Association serves as the statewide leader in CRA education, advocacy, and best practices. Its annual board trainings are recognized as a key resource for ensuring that CRA board members and staff remain informed on evolving legal requirements and industry standards.
The upcoming training in Panama City will provide:
An overview of Florida’s legal framework governing CRAs
Guidance on roles and responsibilities of board members and staff
Best practices for financial management and TIF oversight
Insights into ethical considerations and public transparency
Real-world examples of successful redevelopment strategies
For the City of Milton, continued participation in FRA training opportunities supports the City’s commitment to responsible stewardship of CRA resources and strategic redevelopment across its three CRA districts. As Milton continues to experience growth and increased redevelopment activity, particularly within the Downtown CRA, ongoing education ensures that board members are equipped to make informed, compliant, and impactful decisions.
Funds for this training are available within the CRA 1 budget, consistent with prior year participation. No additional budget amendments are required.
title: FRA CRA Board Training

description:
The City of Milton has a long-standing partnership with the National Naval Aviation Museum (NNAM), serving as a steward of historically significant naval aircraft for public display. For decades, the City has maintained a T-28B Trojan aircraft located at Milton High School under a federal loan agreement. This aircraft has been on display since the mid-1970s and has undergone periodic maintenance. However, due to prolonged exposure to the elements, it has experienced ongoing deterioration.
The City has recently received a loan renewal agreement (2026–2031) for the T-28B, which reaffirms the City’s responsibility to maintain, preserve, and protect the aircraft in accordance with NNAM standards, including all associated costs. These requirements include routine maintenance, corrosion control, and preservation, as well as compliance with strict federal guidelines governing modifications, restoration, and display conditions.
Over time, the T-28B has reached a point where full restoration is necessary. The last available evaluation by NNAM of the plane was conducted in 2018 and the condition at that time was rated as "poor" in all categories (attached). The aircraft contains legacy hazardous paint, requiring specialized abatement before any sanding, welding, or structural repairs. In addition, the aircraft requires extensive fabrication and restoration work to address corrosion and long-term wear. In 2018, the estimated costs for a full restoration project exceeded $250,000. Such a restoration today, would be in the $500,000 range, with ongoing annual maintenance costs of approximately $4,000.
Concurrently, the City has been extended an opportunity by NNAM and Naval Air Station Whiting Field to accept a TH-57C Sea Ranger helicopter for static display. The TH-57 is historically significant to Milton, having served as the primary rotary-wing training aircraft at NAS Whiting Field for decades and playing a direct role in training tens of thousands of Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard aviators. The City formally accepted this aircraft in March 2026. The helicopter is completing the final process for transfer and transport to the City.
In parallel, the City of Foley has expressed interest in acquiring the City’s T-28B aircraft. Foley has proposed to fully fund the relocation, restoration, and long-term indoor preservation of the aircraft within a climate-controlled museum environment, thereby removing the financial and operational burden from the City of Milton.
As part of this transition, the City must also evaluate options for siting and displaying the TH-57C. Preliminary discussions with the City’s engineering firm estimate that construction of a new pedestal could cost approximately $80,000; however, this figure is conceptual only and has not been formally authorized or engineered. Alternatively, if the T-28B is transferred, the City could potentially repurpose the existing pedestal, resulting in significant cost savings.
Any cost for any option chosen is currently not budgeted. Any amount above $10,000 would be funded by utilizing City General Revenue Reserves. This would decrease the reserve funds available for other City priority projects dollar for dollar. Below the $10,000 threshold, staff can identify savings available in the current budget. As expenditures would be expected in the fourth quarter of FY 2026, savings realized throughout the course of the year can be identified and the budget amended for this purpose.
Public input has been solicited regarding these options, and results will be provided to the City Council upon completion.
title: Future of NNAM Aircraft - Static Displays

Appointment of members that are to fill Ward-specific seats should be rated based on favoring those who reside in that Ward, then those that live within the City of Milton, then those that reside in Santa Rosa County, and finally any other criteria supporting the potential members nomination (preference for 1. In ward, 2. In City, 3. In Santa Rosa County).
Council will need to reappoint the eligible members on a 3-year staggered basis. The new "Year One" appointments will need to be scheduled as presented below in the 2 possible scenarios or as Council sees fit. Council will need to decide which stagger scenario is preferred.
After the initial "Year One" rotation, every appointment to every board will be on a 3-year service term, which fulfills the 3-year staggered appointments. (After the first "Year One" 2-year appointments are complete, any future appointment in that seat is on a 3-year rotation)
Each board will have an "Expiration Month". This will create a more cohesive, consistent, and repeatable appointment schedule. Staff recommends: Community Improvement Board - Expiration Month is March with new terms beginning in April. Board of Adjustments - Expiration Month is May and terms beginning in June. Historic Preservation Board - Expiration Month is July with terms beginning in August. Planning Board - Expiration Month September with terms beginning in October.
New appointments after the "Year One" scenario will need to be able to achieve the "Staggered 3-year" term limit. In order to achieve this, the first round of appointments will need to have staggered years of appointments followed by any future appointments being for 3-years. City staff has developed two possible paths in order to do so.
1. 3/4 Seat Stagger - 3 appointments will fill a shortened 2-year term with the usual 3-year term after appointment, and 4 appointments will fill a full 3-year term. This will allow all future 3-year appointments to be staggered in such a manner that 2 consecutive years of appointments will occur with one year of no new appointments. The pattern would repeat; appointments in year four and five, with no new appointments in year six and so on. Again, after the first initial 3, 2-year terms, no more 2-year appointments will be necessary and every appointment from then on will be for the usual 3-years.
2. 2/2/3 Seat Stagger with appointments taking place every year.
In a 2/2/3 Seat Stagger: Group 1 would consist of Ward 1, Council At-Large 1 for one, 1-year term; Group 2 Ward 2, Council At-Large 2 for one, 2-year term; Group 3 Ward 3, Ward 4, Mayor At-Large for one, 3-year term. Each would be appointed for a three-year term thereafter, per usual.
Again, as stated in both scenarios, the non-3-year terms would only occur once, during the "Year One", in order to create the staggered effect. Every appointment after will be the normal 3-year term.
If Council desires, all current Board members can be reappointed to their respective boards under either the 3/4 or 2/2/3 rotation. Staff has developed a recommendation for each seat in each Board with the current membership. This recommendation identifies which seat the current member is filling, and the new term they will serve. If Council adopts this recommendation and the Expiration Month concept, each board will continue as currently configured with the start month for each new term adjusted. Council would not have to make any appointments for any board, other than for vacancies, for one or two years, depending on the rotation schedule selected.

description:
Over the past several years, the City of Milton has made significant investments in downtown revitalization, including enhancements to public spaces, infrastructure improvements, and expanded programming such as community events along the riverfront. These efforts are designed to stimulate private investment, increase foot traffic, and position Milton as a desirable destination for residents, businesses, and visitors.
Despite this progress, many vacant and deteriorating structures remain, creating barriers to continued growth. These properties often:
Remain unmaintained for extended periods
Become targets for vandalism or unauthorized entry
Create safety hazards for adjacent properties and the public
Suppress nearby property values and redevelopment potential
Require disproportionate City resources for monitoring and enforcement
Currently, the City lacks a formal tracking and accountability system specifically for vacant and abandoned properties. Code Enforcement operates actively, addressing complaints as well as proactively managing problem properties, but no formal system is in place to assist them with property information.
This ordinance introduces a structured, enforceable program that:
Identifies and tracks vacant properties through mandatory registration
Requires minimum maintenance and security standards
Assigns clear responsibility to property owners and lenders
Implements a fee structure that incentivizes timely action
Provides Code Enforcement with stronger compliance tools under Chapter 162, Florida Statutes
Additionally, the ordinance aligns with Florida Statute 705.1015, reinforcing local authority to manage abandoned property conditions impacting public welfare.
KEY COMPONENTS OF THE ORDINANCEMandatory Registration:Required for properties vacant for more than 90 days, abandoned properties, and those in foreclosure.
Escalating Fee Structure:Annual fees increase the longer a property remains vacant, incentivizing redevelopment or sale.
Maintenance Requirements:Property owners must secure, maintain, and properly manage properties in compliance with City Code.
Local Contact Requirement:Ensures a responsible party is available for immediate response.
Code Enforcement Administration:Program oversight, inspections, and enforcement are handled by City staff.
STRATEGIC IMPACTThis ordinance supports:
Downtown revitalization and CRA objectives
Economic development and private investment attraction
Public safety and neighborhood stabilization
Efficient use of City resources
It supports Milton to move from reactive enforcement to a proactive redevelopment strategy.
title: Abandoned & Vacant Property Registration Program (City Manager)

description:
Following the Gas Rate Study, staff is requesting Council input on a new fee structure recommended in the study.
The first aspect is the cost of installation. As detailed previously, the City is only charging 10% of the actual cost for installation of a new service. This is unsustainable. Staff recommends that the fee for installation be 100% of the actual cost (labor + materials) adjusted annually. Staff recommends a multiple appliance discount of 10% for new service that staff verify connects more than one appliance to the City's gas service.
The second aspect is a standard monthly service charge. This would be a standardized fee regardless of actual consumption. Currently, the City will complete an installation, incur all costs, minus the 10% connection fee, and the homeowner may never initiate service. As per the Public Service Commission rules, after five years without service, a meter must be removed and the line capped. The City incurs 90% of the installation and 100% of the removal costs and, if service is never initiated, has never billed the customer. The standard charge will also address the limited revenue generated by emergency generators. Staff recommends a minimum monthly service charge of $25.
The final aspect is bringing the rates for service up to the market rates as identified in the Rate Study. The study recommended implementation over time to lessen the burden on customers. Staff recommends a three-year implementation schedule.
Staff recommends the installation fee be adjusted immediately. The standard monthly fee and rate adjustments, staff recommends, be implemented at the start of the fiscal year, October 1, 2026.
title: Natural Gas of Milton Fees

The pickup truck serves a unique and critical role by supporting tasks such as transporting and deploying road barricades during closures, hauling specialized investigative equipment, and moving large recovered property items, including bicycles and other bulky evidence. Given the age, mileage, and increasing maintenance demands of the current vehicle, replacement at this time is both fiscally responsible and operationally necessary. description:
TH-57C Sea Ranger Legacy in MiltonThe TH-57 Sea Ranger was the primary advanced rotary-wing training aircraft at NAS Whiting Field for nearly six decades.
Approximately 34,000–35,000 Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard helicopter pilots earned their Wings of Gold flying the TH-57.
The aircraft logged more than 3.3 million flight hours before its final flight on September 19, 2025.
NAS Whiting Field was the exclusive rotary-wing training site for this aircraft.
The TH-57’s service history is uniquely tied to Milton. Unlike many military aircraft displayed nationwide, this platform only called Milton home for its entire service life. Accepting this aircraft preserves a defining chapter of Milton’s aviation heritage.
Current T-28 Aircraft ConditionThe City’s existing T-28 aircraft has undergone minor cosmetic improvements during its time in Milton. However:
The aircraft contains hazardous legacy paint.
It requires extensive welding and fabrication for structural restoration.
It remains outdoors and exposed to the weather.
The City incurs approximately $4,000 annually in man-hours and repainting costs for maintenance.
The City of Foley has proposed to:
Fully fund the relocation of the T-28 to Foley, Alabama.
Restore the aircraft at their expense.
House the aircraft in a climate-controlled environment.
Assume all future maintenance responsibilities.
This proposal eliminates ongoing maintenance costs and long-term restoration liabilities for the City of Milton.
Strategic Considerations1. Preservation of Local HeritageThe TH-57 represents Milton’s direct and exclusive connection to naval rotary aviation training. Its display reinforces Milton’s identity as the cradle of naval helicopter training.
2. Financial ResponsibilityThe transfer of the T-28 eliminates ongoing annual maintenance expenses and avoids significant future restoration costs associated with hazardous materials and structural rehabilitation.
3. Asset Upgrade Without Capital ExpenseThe City would exchange an aging, maintenance-intensive aircraft for a historically significant platform with deeper local relevance, without acquisition cost.
4. Strengthened Military PartnershipAccepting the TH-57C demonstrates continued partnership with NAS Whiting Field and the National Naval Aviation Museum.
5. Long-Term StewardshipThe T-28 will receive professional restoration and preservation in a controlled environment, ensuring its longevity without financial burden to Milton taxpayers.
title: Acceptance TH-57C Sea Ranger & Transfer T-28B (action item)
