attachments.name: Contractor & Grant New and Revised Position Duties

description:
The City's Grants Division has proven a valuable resource for the City. The Division has generated millions for the City for projects that would have taken years to fund through City revenue streams alone. From the millions for the natural gas line replacement project, and soon to be underway sprayfields and new wastewater treatment plant, to smaller projects like new police equipment, the division generates far and beyond the cost for the staff.
With the recent promotion of the Grants Manager to the Planning Director position, it was the appropriate time to review the Grant Division and determine if the positions align with the needs.
With the additional volume and size of grants secured, and the future anticipated growth in size and complexity of grants, the need for grant administration skill sets has grown over time. The specific identified area of need is in the financial/accounting/reporting area. Grant writing and overall management is managed by the Assistant City Manager with the input and assistance of subject matter specialists throughout the organization. Contracts and compliance sit with the new Contract Coordinator position.
It is recommended that the Grant Manager position be reclassified to a Grant Coordinator position with an emphasis on financial tracking and reporting. This is a different skill set, different education and experience from the Grants Manager Position. This would be a lower level position than the Grant Manager.
The new Contract Coordinator position, approved in the FY 26 Budget, is working well and growing into the role of developing and managing standardized contracts for services and compliance monitoring performance in relation to contracted obligations.
title: Contracts/Grants Revised Position (City Manager)

description:
The City of Milton Community Redevelopment Agency was established to address conditions of deterioration within designated redevelopment areas and to stimulate long-term economic vitality. CRA I (Downtown) was created in 1982, with CRA II North and CRA III South added in 2016 to expand revitalization efforts beyond the historic core.
Under Florida Statutes 163, Part III governing Community Redevelopment Agencies, tax increment revenues are generated from the increase in taxable property values above each district’s established base year. These incremental revenues are reinvested exclusively within the redevelopment areas to fund public improvements, infrastructure, and economic development initiatives.
Over time, the CRA districts have demonstrated significant increases in taxable value and commercial activity. Strategic infrastructure investments, historic preservation efforts, private sector reinvestment, and coordinated planning have contributed to sustained growth within the redevelopment footprint.
While annual TIF revenues may fluctuate based on property valuation cycles and market conditions, long-term trends indicate continued economic productivity within the districts. The CRA’s financial structure, including the prudent use of fund balances carried forward, allows the Agency to plan multi-year projects and respond to emerging redevelopment opportunities.
As the City advances catalytic initiatives such as waterfront redevelopment, business improvement programs, and continued downtown infrastructure improvements, the CRA remains positioned as a central mechanism for guiding responsible growth while preserving Milton’s historic character.
title: Annual Report

description:
For decades, the City of Milton has utilized the same inventory of holiday decorations throughout the Downtown CRA I. Much of this inventory is aging, non-commercial grade, and increasingly unreliable. As a result, City staff annually budgets thousands of dollars to replace lights, repair frames, and patch failing decorative elements. These temporary repairs are becoming more frequent and less effective as the materials continue to deteriorate.
The primary downtown Christmas tree, in particular, has reached the end of its useful life. Due to structural fatigue and mechanical failure, staff must weld components, apply significant force using sledgehammers, and secure the structure with tension straps to achieve proper deployment. These measures present safety concerns for staff and create operational inefficiencies.
At the October 23, 2025, CRA meeting, staff introduced a phased approach to modernize and upgrade Downtown holiday décor. This plan included:
Replacement of the aging primary Christmas tree
Installation of a new tall tree at Jernigan’s Landing
Gradual replacement of outdated and non-commercial grade decorations
Transition to durable, commercial-grade décor to reduce long-term maintenance costs
In Fiscal Year 2024–2025, the CRA initiated Phase I improvements through a purchase with Jubilee Decorations, one of the nation’s largest providers of commercial-grade holiday décor. Jubilee’s proximity (approximately two hours from Milton) provides logistical convenience, service accessibility, and reduced shipping costs.
As previously discussed, staff committed to returning in early 2026 to secure updated pricing for Phase II and III items during the manufacturer’s off-season discount period. The estimate presented today reflects those seasonal savings and results in a cost reduction exceeding $5,000 for the purchase of two new commercial-grade trees.
The proposed investment aligns with the CRA’s mission to enhance the Downtown district, improve aesthetics, support seasonal programming, and create a safe and inviting environment for residents, visitors, and businesses. Additionally, replacing aging infrastructure now will reduce recurring repair expenses, lower staff labor demands, and improve overall operational efficiency.
title: Downtown Decor Purchase

description:
New Board and Committee appointments must now meet the requirements of the ordinances as passed during the 1/13/2026 City Council Meeting. In doing so, each board will need to be reviewed and appointed as Council sees fit. Staff has created a means to do this as a "Year One" scenario. The "Year One" scenario is as described below;
Treat the new 2026 ordinance as a "Year One" appointment ordinance which would allow each member that is eligible to do so, to continue to serve if they so choose to do so and as council appoints them.
Each board will follow the same set-up as the Milton Planning Board - One representative from each ward (as voted on and agreed by the 2 Councils members that represent said Ward), One Mayor at Large appointment, and Two Council At Large appointments for a total of 7 members serving on each board. Currently, the Planning Board is the only City Board that meets the requirements of the new ordinance. The attached spreadsheet shows the deficiencies that must be addressed for each Board to come into compliance with the new requirements. There is also once current Board member who is no longer eligible to serve due to the new requirement to reside in Santa Rosa County. If Council so chooses, the Mayor & Council At-Large seats may be filled with current members. However, current members cannot fill Ward specific seats unless they reside in that Ward according to the new ordinance.
Council will need to reappoint the eligible members on a 3-year staggered basis. The new "Year One" appointments will need to be scheduled as presented below in the 2 possible scenarios or as Council sees fit. Council will need to decide which stagger scenario is preferred.
After the initial "Year One" rotation, every appointment to every board will be on a 3-year service term, which fulfills the 3-year staggered appointments. (After the first "Year One" 2-year appointments are complete, any future appointment in that seat is on a 3-year rotation)
Each board will have an "Expiration Month". This will create a more cohesive, consistent, and repeatable appointment schedule. Staff recommends: Community Improvement Board - Expiration Month is March and appointment beginning in April. Board of Adjuctments - Expiration Month is May and appointment eginning is June. Historic Preservation Board - Expiration Month is July with ppointments beginning in August. Planning Board - Expiration Month September with appointments beginning in October.
New appointments will need to be able to achieve the "Staggered 3-year" term limit. In order to achieve this, the first round of appointments will need to have staggered years of appointments followed by any future appointments being for 3-years. City staff has developed a two possible paths in order to do so.
1. 3/4 Seat Stagger - 3 appointments will fill the usual 3-year term after appointment, and 4 appointments will fill a shortened 2-year term. This will allow all future 3-year appointments to be staggered in such a manner that 2 consecutive years of appointments will occur with one year of no new appointments. The pattern would repeat; appointments in year four and five, with no new appointments in year six and so on.
2. 2/2/3 Seat Stagger with appointments taking place every year.
In a 2/2/3 Seat Stagger: Group 1 would consist of Ward 1, Council At-Large 1 for one, 1-year term; Group 2 Ward 2, Council At-Large 2 for one, 2-year term; Group 3 Ward 3, Ward 4, Mayor At-Large for one 3-year term. Each would be appointed for a three-year term thereafter.
title: Procedures for New Board Appointment Policy Implementation (action item)

description:
All current CIB member seats expire as of 3/1/2026. In order to meet the new Board and Committee Appointment ordinance, specifically 14-25 as approved on 1/13/2026, the Council will need to discuss new appointments for the expiring CIB seats and upcoming vacancies. Currently, 3 members represent Wards 1 and 2 collectively (2 from Ward 1 and 1 from Ward 2). The remaining 4 seats do not represent a ward by a member living in said ward. Per Ordinance 14-25, the board should consist of a representative whose residential address is located within the respective ward(s), one Mayor-at Large, and two Council-at Large for a total of 7 seats. As the board consists now, no representation exists for Ward 3 or Ward 4.
New appointments will need to be able to achieve the "Staggered 3-year" term limit. In order to achieve this, the first round of appointments will need to have staggered years of appointments followed by any future appointments being for 3-years. City staff has developed a two possible paths in order to do so.
1. 3/4 Seat Stagger - 3 appointments will need to fufil the usual 3-year term after appointment, and 4 appointments will need to fulfill a shortened 2-year term. This will allow all future 3-year appointments to be staggered in such a manner that 2 consecutive years of appointments will occur with one year of no new appointments. The pattern would repeat; appointments in year four and five, with no new appointments in year six and so on.
2. 2/2/3 Seat Stagger with appointments taking place every year.
Either scenario would create the need for seat appointment groups. In a 3/4 Seat Stagger, Group 1 would consist of Ward 1, 3, and Council At-Large for one 3-year term. Group 2 would consist of Ward 2, 4, Council-At Large 2 and Mayor-At Large seats for one 2-year term and 3-year terms hereafter.
In a 2/2/3 Seat Stagger: Group 1 Ward 1, Council At-Large 1 for one 2-year term; Group 2 Ward 2, Council At-Large 2 for one 2-year term; Group 3 Ward 3, Ward 4, Mayor At-Large for one 3-year term.

description:
On January 23, 2023, the City of Milton entered into a Consent Order with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. That Consent Order was amended on October 18, 2024 and is currently is in full force and effect. There are two elements within the Amended Consent Order that the City has been unable to come into compliance. The first is a requirement to reduce the level of copper in the treated effluent discharged into the Blackwater River. The City has completed pilot projects to reduce the copper, but have been unable to reach a consistent level below the limitation. The City will be conducting a further pilot study with a new treatment methodology. However, this requirement will become a moot point with the activation of the land-based effluent disposal system, as copper is not regulated on land-based systems. The second requirement is for the City to cease all treated effluent disposal in the Blackwater River by December 31, 2025. A third element that the City is in compliance with but must maintain through April 20, 2028 is to continue to reduce inflow and infiltration (I&I) of stormwater into the sanitary sewer system. The City is continuing to implement various projects to reduce the I&I annually. The City is in compliance with all other aspects of the Amended Consent Order.
The second amendment extends the deadline to achieve compliance with the limits of copper in the effluent discharge by 365 days. The new pilot study will determine if the new methodology meets the requirements in the interim, until the land-based disposal system is activated. The second amendment also extends the deadline to remove all treated effluent from the Blackwater River to December 31, 2032. This aligns the City of Milton with the deadline of all other wastewater plants in Florida. With the recent actions approved by the City to acquire sufficient property and submit permits for a land-based effluent disposal system, the City will far exceed this deadline.
All other aspects of the Amended Consent Order remain unchanged.
Approval of the Second Amended Consent Order will also allow FDEP to complete the operating permit renewal for the existing downtown wastewater treatment plant, as the consent order is a component of that permit.
title: FDEP Second Amended Consent Order

description:
If Council approves the acquisition of the 260 acres for the effluent disposal system, this will bring the total acreage for the project in East Milton to approximately 456 acres. Given the recent notice from FDEP of preliminary approval of the permits to construct the effluent disposal system and collocated new wastewater treatment plant, City staff and BDI believe the time has arrived to begin construction of this project. The first aspect that can proceed in advance of the state permits is the clearing and grubbing of the property where the project will be built. Staff is requesting Council authorization to release a Request for Proposals to clear and grub the project footprint area as defined by BDI. This will include the ingress road on the eastern approach as recently approved by Council. The total area to be cleared is estimated at approximately 450 acres. The clearing and grubbing project is estimated between $1.5 and $3 million and will take approximately one year to complete.
If approved, the RFP will be released in December, with an early January deadline for submission. The resulting low bid will be presented to Council for approval as early as possible in the first quarter of 2026. Council is not obligated to accept a bid or go forward with the project should the situation change.

description:
The City of Milton, Florida, one of Florida's oldest incorporated municipalities and the historic heart of Santa Rosa County, stands at a pivotal moment of growth and transformation. Situated along the pristine Blackwater River, Milton is uniquely positioned to blend its rich heritage with new opportunities for economic expansion, community engagement, and waterfront revitalization.
Over the past decade, the City has strategically invested in public amenities and infrastructure to enhance the quality of life and attract private investment. Projects such as the Jernigan’s Landing Festival Area, Carpenter’s Park Splash Pad, and new recreational additions, including the BMX track and disc golf course, have redefined Milton. At the same time, new commercial developments, including a Publix Shopping Center, numerous QSRs, medical facilities, and the Walmart Market, signal rising market confidence in Milton’s future.
The City’s next major step in this renaissance is the redevelopment of approximately 3.73 acres of City-owned waterfront property on the west bank of the Blackwater River. Historically home to the Milton Marina, these parcels represent a rare opportunity to activate the waterfront with a project that serves as a catalyst for downtown and regional growth. The envisioned development, a combination of marina, restaurant/entertainment, and mixed-use spaces, will connect residents and visitors alike to Milton’s most defining natural asset: the Blackwater River.
Anchored by access to standard municipal utilities and supported by the City’s Community Redevelopment Area (CRA) and Riverfront Master Plan, the Milton Marina project embodies the City’s mission to foster sustainable economic development while preserving Milton’s distinctive small-town charm.

description:
City of Milton Business Improvement Grant Program – Background Report
Program OverviewSince its inception, the City of Milton’s Business Improvement Grant Program has been a driving force in revitalizing local businesses and encouraging private investment within the community. The program provides matching funds to assist property and business owners with exterior improvements that enhance the appearance, functionality, and overall economic vitality of the City.
Program SummaryTotal Projects Funded: 57
Total Requested: $256,692.68
Total Awarded: $256,142.68
Total Required Match (Minimum): $213,926.88
Total Actual Private Investment: $1,727,977.96
CRA Contribution: $117,635.79
City General Fund Contribution: $138,506.89
Return on Investment (ROI)The Business Improvement Grant has generated a significant return on public funds, leveraging private sector investment at a rate of more than 12 times the City’s contribution.
ROI Calculation:
For every $1 invested by the City, participating businesses have invested approximately $6.74 in their properties.

This means every CRA dollar has generated nearly $14.70 in private investment.

description:
The City of Milton is exploring a partnership with the Northwest Florida YMCA to develop a community-scale aquatic and wellness center that would serve residents of Milton and the surrounding areas. This initiative builds upon recent findings from the Santa Rosa County Aquatic Facility Study conducted by BDI in September 2025, and commissioned by Santa Rosa County BoCC, which identified a countywide need for at least two aquatic facilities to meet current and future demand.
Community NeedThe BDI study highlighted several key findings:
Strong community demand for swimming, fitness, and youth aquatic programming.
Limited access to existing facilities—many families must travel to Pensacola or the University of West Florida for swim lessons or competitive training.
A need for community-accessible aquatic centers rather than only competitive or Olympic-scale facilities.
Emphasis on affordability, recreation, and drowning prevention education, especially for youth and veterans.
The City of Milton intends to pursue a smaller, community-focused aquatic center—similar to BDI’s Concept 2 model—which features:
A 7,000-square-foot multipurpose pool with 8 lap lanes
A zero-depth entry area for children and families
Recreational water features with depths ranging from 0 to 7 feet
A compact 3.5 to 5-acre footprint that complements the city’s growing downtown area
Partnership Structure
City of Milton
Owns the facility and provides site development.
Integrates aquatic center with Clyde L. Gracey Community Center expansion.
Creates a central hub for health, recreation, and community programs.
Northwest Florida YMCA
Largest pool operator in the United States.
Operates and manages both the aquatic center and health & wellness center.
Covers all annual operational and maintenance costs.
Offers YMCA membership programs and financial assistance to ensure accessibility.
Brings proven expertise in facility management and community engagement.
Financial SustainabilityYMCA’s dual-use model (aquatics + health & wellness) creates balanced revenue streams.
Membership and program income offset operational costs.
501(c)(3) nonprofit status enables grant funding and scholarships.
Reduces financial burden on city resources while maintaining public ownership.
Community BenefitsProvides year-round aquatic access to residents in and around Milton.
Supports public health, youth development, and senior wellness.
Creates local jobs and volunteer opportunities.
Enhances sports tourism potential through competitive and recreational programming.
Promotes equitable access for families and individuals of all income levels.
title: YMCA Partnership - Milton Aquatic Center

description:
For more than 20 years, the City of Milton has proudly displayed holiday decorations that have become a tradition for residents and visitors alike. However, the city’s current inventory of lights, displays, and garland has reached the end of its useful life.
Many decorations are outdated, costly to maintain, and were originally designed for personal rather than commercial use. Each year, city staff invest significant time and resources into repairs, replacements, and retrofitting older decorations with LED bulbs to extend their life.
The city’s annual budget for holiday decorations is $6,500, which primarily covers maintenance, small replacements, and upgrades to aging materials. While this has kept the display operational, it does not allow for meaningful reinvestment or modernization.

Opening Doors Northwest Florida, Inc. is a nonprofit organization serving as the lead agency and Collaborative Applicant for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Continuum of Care (CoC) funding under CFR 578. In this role, we are responsible for coordinating federal homelessness resources and community planning across our region.

At this time, we are requesting representation from the City of Milton to fill the appointed seat for a local government agency on our Continuum of Care Council. Your voice—and the city’s perspective—are incredibly important as we work to align regional strategies, pursue federal funding opportunities, and respond effectively to homelessness in both urban and rural communities.

description:
ICE’s 287(g) Program The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate to state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under the agency’s direction and oversight.
The 287(g) Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state and local law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the U.S. ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with its law enforcement partners to carry out its critical mission.
The 287(g) program allows ICE, through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.

description:
This is the parade application for Milton's annual Christmas parade, hosted by the Magic Wand Initiative. This will be the second year that this organization runs the parade.
The parade is scheduled for Saturday, December 6th, 2025. The parade will begin staging in the afternoon between 2pm and 4pm. The parade begins at 6pm and will end once the parade reaches its terminus at Elva St.
The parade route sticks to the one we have established in previous years, with staging at the Community Center and Chuck Prince St. The parade will travel to Elva St. by way of James and Stewart Streets. Grace street will serve as the entry road for parade staging.
This event will require closure of Byrom Street between Grace and Sanders Streets for parade staging as well at the closure of James Street and Stewart Street between James Street and Elva Street for the duration of the parade.
For this event, the organizer has requested the following items from the City:Parade Package - $1000.00
Road Closure Package - $100.00
Garbage Can Package - $100.00
Total fees for this event are $1200.00. Due to the organizer's status as a nonprofit organization, these fees are subject to a 50% reduction, bringing the total to $600.00.

description:
On 7/29/2025 the City of Milton officially applied to request $47,932.50 in funding from the Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuaries Program (PPBEP) Community Grant.
The City of Milton, in partnership with the University of West Florida, proposes a collaborative project to restore and enhance a stormwater-connected tributary and stream system feeding into the Blackwater River, an Outstanding Florida Water. The project will address severe sedimentation, unmanaged street and recreational water runoff, and wetland overgrowth, which are degrading water quality and increasing direct untreated discharges into the river.By leveraging academic expertise, local knowledge, and a science-driven approach, the project aims to identify sources and pathways of sediment, clarify ownership and maintenance responsibilities of the stream, perform comprehensive water and soil quality assessments of the stream, and develop a community-supported remediation and restoration plan for the Blackwater River associated stream.
The PPBEP Council has requested that no media coverage be provided at this time and PPBEP will roll out their own press release after the Sept. 25th PPBEP Grants Symposium.
title: Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuaries Program Community Grant (action item)

description:
MPD is requesting the acquisition of collapsible high-visibility traffic safety cones for use by our officers in the field, particularly at crash scenes and roadside incidents. These cones are an essential tool to enhance officer safety, manage vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and clearly mark hazardous zones during emergency response situations.
These modern collapsible cones offer several distinct advantages over traditional models:High Visibility: Designed in bright safety orange with 360-degree reflective stripes, these cones offer outstanding visibility during both daytime and nighttime operations, making them highly effective in alerting approaching drivers to the presence of emergency responders.
Portable and Foldable: The collapsible design allows the cones to be stored compactly in the trunk of patrol cars using the included carrying bag. This ensures quick and easy access when needed, without taking up excessive space.
Sturdy and Reliable: Each cone has a 10x10 inch base for stability on various road surfaces. This ensures they remain upright even in less-than-ideal weather or road conditions, clearly delineating work zones for officers and other first responders.
Durable Construction: Made from high-quality Oxford fabric and molded PP materials, these cones are waterproof, fade-resistant, and built to withstand prolonged exposure to the elements without losing their effectiveness.
Versatile Use: These cones can be deployed quickly for traffic crashes, road closures, crowd control, parking enforcement, or for direct traffic during special events.
The use of traffic cones significantly increases officer safety by providing a visible barrier, redirecting vehicle flow, and establishing safe working zones. Officers working roadside are among the most vulnerable, and these cones serve as a critical tool to reduce the risk of injury from passing motorists.
title: Council Discretionary Funds Balance FY25 Budget to Purchase MPD Equipment (action item)

description: Three years ago, City Council adopted Ordinance 1981-22. This Ordinance amended Section 36, Article III of the city code and allowed for limited placement of food trucks across our community based on a lease agreement. Since the ordinance passed, the program has remained stagnant. Only one vendor expressed any interest in the program as codified, and that interest waned rapidly after trialing the lease. Simply put, the program is ineffective because it tries to treat mobile vendors the same as brick-and-mortar businesses. As designed, it forces mobile vendors to stay in one place while the entire purpose of a mobile vendor is to flit about and go to where the customers are on a seasonal basis. After three years of running the City's events program and countless dialogues with residents, mobile vendor operators, and members of City staff, I would like to request that the Council review this ordinance and see if we can find ways to make this program more practical. Notably, I would strongly recommend that the City move away from a long-term lease program and instead focus on daily rentals. A daily rental program could easily be managed through Park's & Recreation's CivicRec program, similar to park pavilion rentals. This would, for example, allow an ice cream truck or snow cone vendor to consider setting up in Carpenter's park on a hot summer day. They could go online, select the date they want, pay the fee through the Parks website, and then go conduct their business. All without putting additional strain on City personnel or resources. As our ordinance currently stands, that same vendor would need to fill out a large amount of paperwork which needs to be reviewed by staff. They would then need to take out an annual lease and pay an exorbitant fee. They would then need to abide by the somewhat arbitrary and restrictive terms of the lease, including the stipulation that they must operate at that location a minimum of 20 hours per month. Yes, the snow cone vendor would be required to set up shop in winter months when their sales would be nonexistent. In addition to the lease terms being unattractive to vendors, we provide nothing in the way of amenities for the leaseholder. The 10 vendor spots outlined in 1981-22 do not provide any electrical or water connections. In fact, the lease outright forbids leaseholders from making use of city electrical outlets, water spigots, and trash cans. So the only thing they get for their money is space. Page 65 of 67 page 2 of 2 But, we haven't created those spaces. In the list of outlined locations, some mention that the vendor cannot be located in or on the designated parking areas. Ideally, we would provide a pad for these vehicles to park on so that they are stable and level and not sitting on the grass. If the vendor is paying a use fee, we should also look to provide power, water, and trash cans to help keep the area clean and limit noise pollution from loud generators. To this end, I have made a request to the CRA to construct a food truck pad at Carpenter's Park. This pad would serve as a trial basis for pads to be installed at some of the other locations.
title: Ordinance No. 07-25 Mobile Vending Ordinance Update (2nd Reading)

description:
The City of Milton's Investment Policy is found beginning on page 27 of the FY 2025 Budget Book. The City's Policy is attached to this item. The highlighted yellow section is section 2-695 Delegation of authority: designating the CFO as the manager of the City's investments.
Staff has researched the best practices for municipal investment policies as recommended by the Government Finance Officer's Association, the recognized expert in the field. Staff also collected the investment policies from several surrounding local governments, including Escambia and Santa Rosa Counties and the Cities of Pensacola, Gulf Breeze, Destin, Crestview and Ft. Walton Beach. The City of Milton's policy mirrors, or is identical, to the surrounding governments and is consistent with the GFOA best practice recommendations. GFOA recommends the governing body set the policy and strategies and delegate authority to the appropriate individuals to manage the portfolio. This aids in preventing conflicts of interest, ensuring the knowledge and skills necessary to manage the investments, and oversight of the investments in conformance with the policy. For the City of Milton, the City Council sets the policy; The CFO is delegated full authority to manage the investments, but is not authorized to actually open accounts or move funds. The City Clerk and/or Mayor are authorized to open accounts and move funds. This provides an additional level of security and accountability.
title: Investment Policy (Farrow)

The program also increases engagement in the Community Redevelopment Area (CRA), as youth receive and redeem their free ice cream cone coupons at participating local businesses. description: Three years ago, City Council adopted Ordinance 1981-22. This Ordinance amended Section 36, Article III of the city code and allowed for limited placement of food trucks across our community based on a lease agreement. Since the ordinance passed, the program has remained stagnant. Only one vendor expressed any interest in the program as codified, and that interest waned rapidly after trialing the lease. Simply put, the program is ineffective because it tries to treat mobile vendors the same as brick-and-mortar businesses. As designed, it forces mobile vendors to stay in one place while the entire purpose of a mobile vendor is to flit about and go to where the customers are on a seasonal basis. After three years of running the City's events program and countless dialogues with residents, mobile vendor operators, and members of City staff, I would like to request that the Council review this ordinance and see if we can find ways to make this program more practical. Notably, I would strongly recommend that the City move away from a long-term lease program and instead focus on daily rentals. A daily rental program could easily be managed through Park's & Recreation's CivicRec program, similar to park pavilion rentals. This would, for example, allow an ice cream truck or snow cone vendor to consider setting up in Carpenter's park on a hot summer day. They could go online, select the date they want, pay the fee through the Parks website, and then go conduct their business. All without putting additional strain on City personnel or resources. As our ordinance currently stands, that same vendor would need to fill out a large amount of paperwork which needs to be reviewed by staff. They would then need to take out an annual lease and pay an exorbitant fee. They would then need to abide by the somewhat arbitrary and restrictive terms of the lease, including the stipulation that they must operate at that location a minimum of 20 hours per month. Yes, the snow cone vendor would be required to set up shop in winter months when their sales would be nonexistent. In addition to the lease terms being unattractive to vendors, we provide nothing in the way of amenities for the leaseholder. The 10 vendor spots outlined in 1981-22 do not provide any electrical or water connections. In fact, the lease outright forbids leaseholders from making use of city electrical outlets, water spigots, and trash cans. So the only thing they get for their money is space. Page 65 of 67 page 2 of 2 But, we haven't created those spaces. In the list of outlined locations, some mention that the vendor cannot be located in or on the designated parking areas. Ideally, we would provide a pad for these vehicles to park on so that they are stable and level and not sitting on the grass. If the vendor is paying a use fee, we should also look to provide power, water, and trash cans to help keep the area clean and limit noise pollution from loud generators. To this end, I have made a request to the CRA to construct a food truck pad at Carpenter's Park. This pad would serve as a trial basis for pads to be installed at some of the other locations.

description:
The City of Milton's Investment Policy is found beginning on page 27 of the FY 2025 Budget Book. The City's Policy is attached to this item. The highlighted yellow section is section 2-695 Delegation of authority: designating the CFO as the manager of the City's investments.
Staff has researched the best practices for municipal investment policies as recommended by the Government Finance Officer's Association, the recognized expert in the field. Staff also collected the investment policies from several surrounding local governments, including Escambia and Santa Rosa Counties and the Cities of Pensacola, Gulf Breeze, Destin, Crestview and Ft. Walton Beach. The City of Milton's policy mirrors, or is identical, to the surrounding governments and is consistent with the GFOA best practice recommendations. GFOA recommends the governing body set the policy and strategies and delegate authority to the appropriate individuals to manage the portfolio. This aids in preventing conflicts of interest, ensuring the knowledge and skills necessary to manage the investments, and oversight of the investments in conformance with the policy. For the City of Milton, the City Council sets the policy; The CFO is delegated full authority to manage the investments, but is not authorized to actually open accounts or move funds. The City Clerk and/or Mayor are authorized to open accounts and move funds. This provides an additional level of security and accountability.
title: Investment Policy (discussion)

Grants Update - Upcoming Applications
This is an informational item only and serves as an update to the possible grants that the City of Milton's Grants Team is pursuing.
1. Opioid Settlement Fund - DCF - Funds associated with the Florida Opioid Settlement have been earmarked for municipal uses associated with education, harm reduction, and support as it pertains to opioids. The City of Milton was previously appropriated $43,308.84. We are currently in the process of applying to DCF to expend those funds on AEDs for MPD, Deterra Bags for drug disposal, and a public outreach campaign on appropriate disposal techniques.

This grant aims to remedy the aging infrastructure, provide improved services through City-owned and maintained infrastructure, and work to build a relationship with Whiting Field and the DoD personnel that serve in our area.
4. PHMSA TAG Program - PHMSA/DOT - Milton is in the early stages or researching possible drone equipment and accompanying software for gas line leaks and safety inspections. This is part of our FGU membership and would set Milton Gas apart as one of the first adopters of drones as part of utility safety in the area.

description:
At the request of Council, staff reviewed the City's current severance pay liability. Currently, all severance amounts are negotiated individually. For the 21 contract positions within the City, there is a total liability of 166 weeks of severance. The average is 7.9 weeks per contract employee. The range is from 20 weeks severance to zero severance. The attached spreadsheet details the current liability. The chart also shows two hypothetical scenarios for standardizing the severance across the City. There is a "High" and "Low" hypothetical. The High scenario details a severance varying from a high of 20 weeks to a low of 12 weeks. The Low scenario details a severance that varies from a high of 20 to a low of 8 weeks. Both the Low and High scenarios result is a higher liability for severance that the current, negotiated total. The High scenario results in 300 weeks of severance across the 21 contract positions (80.7% increase over current liability). The Low scenario results in 228 weeks (37.3% increase over current liability).
If the City were to uniformly apply the same amount of severance across all 21 positions, it would result in all positions receiving 8 weeks of severance to achieve the same liability as today's independently negotiated, varying amounts. This is equal to the current average of 7.9 weeks. A policy of standardizing severance would also create inequities based on tenure. For example, if standardized, a brand-new contact employee, such as our new Police Chief, would receive the same amount of severance as the Fire Chief, who has been with the City nearly 30 years.
Utilizing severance as a negotiation aspect, which is one component of a complete compensation package, provides the flexibility to meet the specific needs of a prospective City Employee. For example, one candidate may wish to negotiate for relocation expenses in exchange for reduced severance. Another may wish to maximize the protection severance affords at the expense of other considerations.
If Council were to consider a severance standardization policy, staff would recommend "up to" amounts be stipulated, based on the level of the position. This would still allow flexibility in negotiation. Such a plan may be organized as follows:
City Manager - Up to 20 weeks
Assistant City Manager - Up to 16 weeks
Department Director - Up to 12 weeks
Other Contract Employees - Up to 8 weeks
If such a plan were considered, it should apply to all new hires after a future start date and not impact the terms and conditions of existing contracts.
title: Severance Pay Review (Farrow)

description:
Three years ago, City Council adopted Ordinance 1981-22. This Ordinance amended Section 36, Article III of the city code and allowed for limited placement of food trucks across our community. This ordinance also identified numerous locations throughout the City where food trucks could be placed. However, these locations lack water and electrical connections, which are crucial to making these locations desirable for mobile vendors.
After numerous conversations with residents, vendors, and City staff, I would like to recommend that we install a food truck pad at one of the locations identified in the ordinance. I believe that Carpenter's Park would provide the best location for a food truck pad trial program.
Simply put, I would like to ask the CRA to consider allocating funding for the construction of a food truck pad at Carpenter's Park adjacent to the restroom/pump house building. The entrance to the pad would be a pre-existing gate along Munson Highway. Construction of the pad would be done using permeable pavers to avoid issues with our storm water management plan. Next to the pad, I would like to see a power pole with two 50-amp outlets installed as well as an additional pole providing water spigots. Finally, I would like to place two trash cans next to the pad and install a wooden fence to shield them from view of the splash pad.
This request is being paired with a recommendation to the City Council for changes to the City's mobile vendor lease agreement. Those changes, if approved, would allow for daily rentals of the food truck pads, managed through Parks & Recreation's CivicRec rental site, and would provide a regular source of revenue for the CRA to fund additional projects.
title: Food Truck Pad at Carpenter's Park

description: At the February City Council meeting, Council requested a policy to specify the process for receiving legal service of process by the City. Staff researched the issue and drafted the attached policy. The City Charter stipulates the Mayor shall receive service of process, but there is no reference to whom shall receive service in the absence of the Mayor. State Statute 48.111 Service on Public Agencies and Officers, provides that guidance. description:
At the request of City Council, staff asked the former City attorney for, "all phone logs, emails, text messages, social media or other communication that are City public records, be submitted to the City for archiving and preservation in accordance with state statute".
In response, the former City Attorney replied via email on March 12, 2025:
"that is an incredibly broad scope with no time range identified. Is there a date range being requested? I can certainly sift through my text messages and phone call logs for all records of phone calls and texts with city officials dating as far back as my phone bills are available, but that is work only I can do. I estimate that the time to pull, identify, and redact exempt or non-public records would take a good part of a day. I would bill the City at my previous rate with the City of $250, instead of my normal hourly rate of $350. I'd have to invoice for $2,000 to pull together that public records request."
Fees for the production of public records are allowed by the Public Records Act (FS 119.07(4)) and reasonable deposits prior to conducting the work are also allowed.
Staff is requesting Council direction on this matter.
title: Fee for Public Records

attachments.name: Milton CRA Annual Report 2024 - email and web version

description:
The Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) is required by Florida law to submit an annual report on its activities and financial performance to the State by March 31st of each year. This requirement is outlined in Section 163.371 of the Florida Statutes, which mandates that each CRA provide a report detailing its redevelopment efforts, financial expenditures, and overall impact within the designated CRA district.
The report serves several key purposes:
Transparency & Accountability – Demonstrates how taxpayer funds are allocated and spent.
Progress & Impact – Highlights the CRA’s redevelopment initiatives, projects, and improvements within the district.
Compliance – Ensures adherence to state reporting requirements and maintains the CRA’s eligibility for funding and operational continuity.
The 2024 CRA Annual Report will showcase significant achievements from the past year, including economic development projects, infrastructure improvements, and preservation efforts that contribute to the city's historic charm and ongoing growth. Upon completion, the report will be submitted to the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity (DEO) and made available to the public, ensuring continued transparency in the CRA’s efforts.
This presentation provides an overview of the report’s contents and the steps taken to fulfill this statutory requirement.
title: Milton CRA Annual Report 2024

description:
In 2009, the City of Milton acquired a 24.863-acre parcel of land from Santa Rosa County for the purpose of constructing a new wastewater treatment facility (Parcel #29-2N-27-0000-00103-0000). The recent decision by City Council to relocate the new plant to a different location has made this parcel unnecessary for the wastewater project. As such, the City would have no present or future use or need for the property. Selling the property would provide funds that can be applied toward the cost of relocating, redesigning and re-permitting the facility at a new location or provide funds to purchase additional property to meet the needs of the new design. The City will retain a 30-foot easement on the eastside of the parcel for the future Whiting Field Force Main Pipeline, should that project come to pass.
Staff recommends issuing an Invitation to Bid as the disposal method. This method would result in sealed bids wherein each bidder would submit their best price for the property. Council would have the option to accept or reject the bid.
Council has the following options:
1. Do nothing and maintain ownership of the property. This would require the City to maintain liability for any activities that may occur on the property.
2. Donate the property to an eligible entity for their use.
3. List the property with the City's contracted real estate firm for marketing and sale.
4. Issue a Request for Proposals which would incorporate the sale price along with consideration of the future use.
5. Issue an Invitation to Bid to dispose of the property to the highest bidder.

Res 2025-02 Public Records Exemption for City Clerks

description:
The Florida Association of City Clerks (FACC) Board of Directors is considering how to pursue state legislation to provide a public records exemption for the personal information of current Municipal Clerks and employees who perform municipal elections work.
Many municipal staff who perform duties that include, or result in, investigations into complaints regarding election fraud, legal enforcement of hearings related to neglect or abuse, or other activities that could lead to a criminal prosecution are exposed to threats and other acts of violence.
Municipal Clerks often administer elections. Some election workers have been targeted for threats and violence due to the nature of materials they are responsible for. Further, Clerks are often involved in legal enforcement proceedings in actions related to violations of codes and ordinances. Occasionally, these proceedings have led to retaliation and threats by defendants.
Please note, there are currently 27 public record exemptions for specific roles, one of which applies to Code Enforcement Officers. Code Officers are covered by the exemption, but not Municipal Clerks. There is language referencing code enforcement work in the resolution template for the purpose of including Municipal Clerks and employees who perform work related to code enforcement proceedings to be included as part of the public record exemption.
title: Resolution# 2025-02 Public Records Exemption for City Clerks

description: The City's 2018 front loader commercial garbage truck has been out of service since December 2024 due to a factory recall for steering and rear-end issues. This vehicle services our commercial dumpster customers 5 days/week. The City's second front end loader is utilized 2 days/week. This vehicle is a 2001 unit with 152,800 miles and is not reliable enough to utilize daily. Since December 2024, the City has rented a front end loader to ensure service for our customers. This rental vehicle is a 2017 model with 6,600 miles and is in like new with a warranty. The City has been offered the opportunity to purchase this unit for $198,012.50. A portion of the 2 month rental payments will be applied to the purchase price. The FY 2025 budget has an allocation of $500,000 to purchase a new unit. The City received a quote on January 30, 2025 for a new unit. The cost for a new vehicle is $415,210. Due to the low mileage, warranty and like new condition, staff recommends Council authorize purchase of the used unit and declare the 2001 unit as surplus to sell. When repaired the 2018 unit will become the back-up unit. This action, if approved, will save the City $217,197.50.
title: Purchase of Front Loader Sanitation Truck (action item)

description:
In 2009, the City of Milton acquired a 24.863-acre parcel of land from Santa Rosa County for the purpose of constructing a new wastewater treatment facility (Parcel #29-2N-27-0000-00103-0000). The recent decision by City Council to relocate the new plant to a different location has made this parcel unnecessary for the wastewater project. As such, the City would have no present or future use or need for the property. Selling the property would provide funds that can be applied toward the cost of relocating, redesigning and re-permitting the facility at a new location or provide funds to purchase additional property to meet the needs of the new design. The City will retain a 30-foot easement on the eastside of the parcel for the future Whiting Field Force Main Pipeline, should that project come to pass.
Staff recommends issuing an Invitation to Bid as the disposal method. This method would result in sealed bids wherein each bidder would submit their best price for the property. Council would have the option to accept or reject the bid.
Council has the following options:
1. Do nothing and maintain ownership of the property. This would require the City to maintain liability for any activities that may occur on the property.
2. Donate the property to an eligible entity for their use.
3. List the property with the City's contracted real estate firm for marketing and sale.
4. Issue a Request for Proposals which would incorporate the sale price along with consideration of the future use.
5. Issue an Invitation to Bid to dispose of the property to the highest bidder.
title: Declaration of Surplus Property - 24-Acre Parcel (action item)

description:
In 2014, the City of Milton selected NAI Halford to serve as the City's real estate broker for any and all land transactions. The contract with NAI Halford has been renewed annually since that time. Staff can find no record of any renewal being approved by City Council. The use of a third party realtor is preferred to avoid any real or perceived conflict of interest surrounding property transactions and the City's elected officials or staff. NAI Halford has provided quality services, fulfilled every obligation to the City and gone above and beyond their contractual obligations.
City is at critical time wherein multiple property transactions are ongoing, including a property swap for land to build a new water tower and well at Whisper Creek and the ongoing need for land to serve as sprayfields. The expertise and time necessary to carry out these real estate transactions is not available with current City staff. However, staff recognized the need to competitively solicit services on a regular cycle to ensure competition, quality and cost effectiveness. As such, staff is recommending Council approve a one year renewal of the contract between the City and NAI Halford at the current terms and conditions and in July, 2025, issue a new Request for Qualifications for future real estate services. NAI Halford would be eligible to compete under the new RFQ. Further, staff recommends a maximum contract of three to five years for the chosen company.
title: NAI Pensacola Contract Renewal (action item)

description:
The historic Exchange Hotel at 5185 Elmira Street houses Blackwood Financial Group's downtown offices. The applicant acquired the property in 2024 for $750,000 through an ownership entity identified in the application materials as Peace Train Holdings LLC. The adjacent parcel at 5181 Elmira Street, which contains a small building and employee parking, is also identified as being held by a similarly named entity. The legal ownership name should be confirmed against the current application and property records before final publication.
Richard McCool, the owner, has applied for CRA business improvement assistance for improvements to these properties in each of the past three years. The awards supported improvements to the historic building and the adjacent staff-support property. In each year, the required match was lower than the reported project spending.
Grant History and Reported Project SpendingYearPropertyCRA Award / Required MatchReported Project Spending20245185 Elmira Street$10,000 / $7,500About $90,000 for doors and windows20255185 Elmira Street$10,000 / $7,500More than $27,50020255181 Elmira Street​$5,000 / $2,500$4,35520265185 Elmira Street$7,500 approved (from $10,000 request) / $2,500More than $21,000 for painting
Three-year totals: CRA awards of $32,500; required applicant matches totaling $20,000; and reported project spending exceeding $142,855. Reported spending is compared with grant awards as a program-output measure; the source figures do not identify the grant-funded share of each project cost.
Amendment 3 and the Commercial Tax Base
Florida voters approved Amendment 3 in November 2026, and it takes effect January 1, 2027. It increases the homestead exemption for non-school taxes and reduces the annual assessment cap for non-homestead properties, including commercial property, from 10% to 5%. The City’s current local estimate indicates that 1,958 of 2,051 homesteaded homes (95.47%) would receive an increased exemption. This is a count of affected homesteaded homes, not a finding that 96% of residential ad valorem value or revenue will be eliminated.
As the increased homestead exemption is expected to reduce the City’s ad valorem revenue, the strength and condition of the commercial tax base become increasingly important to long-term fiscal resilience. Commercial property improvements can support reinvestment and contribute to the marketability and condition of downtown properties. The Blackwood projects demonstrate how CRA assistance has been paired with larger reported improvement activity at two downtown parcels.

description:
Sullivan Wickley purchased the Six Flags Shopping Center on September 10, 2026, for a reported $11.6 million. Staff has identified the transaction as the largest land purchase within Milton’s city limits. The property’s continued operation and reinvestment may support the City’s commercial tax base and future ad valorem revenues.
In its request to the City, Sullivan Wickley described a broader plan to reposition the center and improve its appearance and marketability.
The anticipated work includes replacing the roof, improving landscaping, removing trash and debris, addressing parking-lot flooding, repairing the parking area, modernizing the pylon sign, enhancing the façade, and repainting the center. The owner noted that final work will depend on project economics, contractor pricing, and tenant discussions.
The owner reports that work began soon after the purchase. Reported investments include approximately $2.9 million for roof replacement, addressing an aging roof covering about 70 percent of the center; approximately $2.5 million in tenant improvements to attract national tenants; and approximately $200,000 for structural work to support columns and return vacant spaces to marketability. Sullivan Wickley’s stated goal is to modernize the facility and attract national retail tenants.
John Murphy, the company’s CFO, requested a façade grant of $25,000 per year for two years. He proposed tying the grant to repainting the center because the work is clearly defined and can be verified, and he indicated that the painting cost would exceed the proposed $50,000 grant. The grant would support this discrete improvement within a larger private redevelopment effort.
The request reached the City in September 2026. Staff hoped to bring it forward in October, but the local response to Hurricane Isaias delayed the item. Since then, Florida voters have approved Amendment 3. Beginning with the 2027 tax roll, the amendment increases the homestead exemption for non-school taxes and reduces the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10 percent to 5 percent. It also changes the constitutional provisions governing the use of county and municipal ad valorem revenue.
These changes add pressure to the City’s long-term revenue outlook and make the strength of Milton’s commercial property base increasingly important. The City cannot assume residential property will continue to support General Fund needs at the same level. At the same time, any proposed General Fund grant should be reviewed against available funding, applicable program requirements, and the restrictions that apply to the proposed revenue source before the City makes a commitment.
If the building is assessed at $10,000,000, it will generate $41,180 in ad valorem taxes for the City annually.

description:
The existing community center serves as a recreation facility and as an evacuation shelter for Santa Rosa County. The City’s experience during the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted limitations in the facility’s ability to support safe operations during a public health emergency. More recently, Hurricane Isaias underscored that the center’s age and condition limit its suitability as a hurricane evacuation shelter. Experiences such as these prompted the City to consider how the facility could better support residents during natural disasters and public health emergencies, while continuing to meet everyday community needs.
The City team began by identifying the facility’s recreational needs and the services residents would like to see. Feasibility and market needs assessments indicated a need for expanded services and greater flexibility in how the center is used. Staff and GMC then worked to develop a design that responds to those needs while incorporating emergency shelter and resiliency functions and remaining mindful of the City’s project budget goal.
GMC’s scope includes planning and design for the expansion and renovation, with architectural and engineering services covering civil, structural, mechanical, plumbing, fire protection, and electrical disciplines. GMC’s work has been structured in two phases. Phase 1 includes program definition, review of existing building and site conditions, preliminary and design development documents, grant solicitation materials, and initial cost estimating. Phase 2 is intended to include completion of construction documents for bidding and permitting, coordination during pricing and bidding, and construction administration. Accordingly, Council’s review of the current design supports the project’s continued development; bidding and construction will require completion of the applicable Phase 2 work and project funding.
GMC’s October 2026 fee update states that the Phase 1 professional fee remains $500,000, with a revised internal allocation among surveying and related investigations, architectural and engineering services, and cost estimating.

description: As response efforts to Hurricane Isaias continue, planning and development have received a great deal of inquiries regarding permitting structures which legally existed before Hurricane Isaias. Typically and in line with other agencies in the state, municipalities would waive review and permitting fees associated with rebuilding hurricane-damaged, legally existing, non-altered structures for the period of the local declaration of an emergency. This ordinance allows for such fees to be waived as long as the individual seeking the waiver is building the asset back "one-for-one" in the same footprint as it existed prior to Hurricane Isaias. This ordinance would automatically repeal when the declaration of emergency ends.
title: Emergency Ordinance # 20-26 - Review and Fee Waivers for Hurricane Related Damages
